The large seed of an avocado
The hard stone of a mango
hints: Karol G and Nicki Minaj used it in a song about heartbreak, but here we mean the literal thing.
You throw it away after eating, and it comes from a plant whose food grows wrapped in leaves.
It's what's left in your hand when you finish a grilled ear from a street cart in the park.
questions.description: A word that works just as well for a broken heart as for Grandma's kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: That's why Colombians say someone «está con la tusa»: they're left empty, like the cob after all the kernels have been eaten.

questions.question: Complete: Grupo Niche is to “Cali pachanguero” as Fruko y sus Tesos is to…
hints: The song was recorded by the Discos Fuentes label from Medellín.
It was sung by Wilson “Saoko” Manyoma, in a mournful voice.
It tells the story of someone locked up in a jail.
questions.description: A classic danced so often in December that it should have its own ID card and a pension by now.
questions.fun_fact: The great Joe Arroyo began his career singing with Fruko y sus Tesos before starting his own orchestra.

questions.question: Near Lake Maracaibo, the Catatumbo lightning flashes almost every night in the same spot. What did sailors use it for?
questions.answer: As a lighthouse to find their way
wrong_answers: As a clock to tell the time
As a warning of a hurricane
As a sign that pirates were near
hints: Think about what a ship needs when everything is dark.
What makes it useful is that the flashes always appear in the same spot and can be seen from very far away.
Sailors named it after the towers with lights that stand on coasts.
questions.description: A storm that works overtime almost every night of the year and never asks for a vacation.
questions.fun_fact: The Catatumbo lightning can produce thousands of flashes in a single night, and from far away you can hardly hear the thunder.

questions.question: I'm a saying grandmas repeat when troubles are finally over. I start like this: “After the storm comes the…”. What word do I end with?
hints: Think about how everything feels when the storm finally goes away.
It also describes a sea with no waves and no wind.
It rhymes with “palm” and means peace and quiet.
questions.description: A saying for days when everything goes wrong… until it stops going wrong.
questions.fun_fact: Many languages share this saying, and Spanish has an equally famous version: “After the storm, the sun comes out.”

questions.question: What is the outermost layer of the atmosphere called, where the air fades into space and some atoms escape?
hints: It is much higher up than where airplanes fly.
It begins above the height where the International Space Station circles Earth.
Its name starts with a Greek prefix that means “outside.”
questions.description: The top floor of Earth's air: no railings, but a great view of space.
questions.fun_fact: By some definitions, the exosphere reaches up to about 10,000 km (6,200 mi), only about 3% of the way to the Moon.

questions.question: What do you call a river mouth that splits into many branches and forms a triangle, like the Nile's?
hints: The same word is also used in math and physics.
It is named after a Greek letter shaped like a triangle.
It is the fourth letter of the Greek alphabet: alpha, beta, gamma…
questions.description: A river so long that by the end it gets tired and spreads out like a fan.
questions.fun_fact: The Greek historian Herodotus called the mouth of the Nile a “delta” because it looked like the Greek letter Δ.

questions.question: I'm shaped like a tower with a metal ring on top, and Nikola Tesla invented me. What am I for?
wrong_answers: Cooling the air in a room
hints: My inventor worked with electricity his whole life.
When I'm switched on, I give off sparks that look like lightning.
My bolts jump through the air because the electricity I make pushes with enormous force.
questions.description: An invention that makes even the most bored parents at a museum pull out their phones to film it.
questions.fun_fact: Some Tesla coils can “sing”: by changing the rhythm of their sparks, they play tunes you can hear in the air.

questions.question: At the ancient Greek Olympic Games, winners got a crown of branches instead of medals. Which tree were the branches from?
hints: It was a tree sacred to the goddess Athena.
It's a typical Mediterranean tree with silvery leaves.
Its fruit gives an oil that is very famous in cooking.
questions.description: A prize you couldn't keep in a display case, because it dried up in a few weeks.
questions.fun_fact: At the Athens 2004 Olympics, winners also received olive crowns, as a tribute to the ancient Games.

questions.question: Every year, more than a million wildebeest, zebras and gazelles travel in a big loop through the Serengeti and the Maasai Mara. Why?
questions.answer: To follow the rains and fresh grass
wrong_answers: To escape fires on the savanna
To look for salt in the mountains
To find shade in the rainforest
hints: The African savanna has dry seasons and rainy seasons.
Wildebeest are plant-eaters and eat a huge amount every day.
Where it rains, the food they need starts to grow.
questions.description: More than a million travelers with no suitcases, no GPS and no stops for gas.
questions.fun_fact: During the migration, hundreds of thousands of wildebeest calves are born within a few weeks, and they can walk just minutes after birth.

questions.question: Its name comes from a Russian word meaning “white.” What is this Arctic whale called?
hints: It lives in icy waters near the North Pole.
Sailors called it the “canary of the sea” because of its whistles and squeaks.
Its name starts with “Be…” and has three syllables.
questions.description: A Russian name for an animal that has never set foot in Moscow.
questions.fun_fact: Belugas are born gray and slowly turn white as they grow up.

questions.question: In which city was Antonio Vivaldi, the composer of “The Four Seasons”, born?
hints: It is in northern Italy, on the Adriatic Sea.
It is famous for its carnival of masks.
Instead of streets it has canals, and people get around by gondola.
questions.description: Spring, summer, fall and winter: a musician who never had to go shopping for inspiration.
questions.fun_fact: Vivaldi was called “il Prete Rosso”, the Red Priest, because he was a priest with red hair.

questions.question: What is the name of the camera that shows how hot everything is, with cold things in blue and hot things in yellow?
hints: Firefighters also use it to see through smoke.
It can also find animals hiding in the middle of the night.
Its name shares a root with “thermometer” and with the “thermos” that keeps your coffee hot.
questions.description: A photo where nobody shows up in their real colors, not even the volcano.
questions.fun_fact: With thermal cameras, volcanologists can notice a crater heating up before the volcano erupts.

questions.question: I'm Ryan, from the channel “Ryan's World”. I started on YouTube at age 3 and became the world's top-earning YouTuber. What kind of videos made me famous?
hints: What he did is what any kid does on Christmas morning.
Companies sent him boxes and boxes of stuff to show off.
He opened boxes, took out what was inside, played with it and said if he liked it.
questions.description: A kid who made more money before learning to tie his shoes than your dad will in his whole life.
questions.fun_fact: Forbes magazine named Ryan the world's highest-paid YouTuber in 2018 and 2019, when he was only about 7 or 8 years old.

questions.question: This volcano is Anak Krakatau, the “child of Krakatoa.” In which country is it?
hints: It is in Asia, in a country made up of thousands of islands.
It lies between the islands of Java and Sumatra.
The country's capital is Jakarta.
questions.description: Like father, like son: just as explosive.
questions.fun_fact: The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa was heard almost 4,800 km (3,000 miles) away, on islands in the Indian Ocean.

questions.question: In 1816, it snowed in June in Europe because of ash from Tambora, a volcano in Indonesia. Roughly how far is it from Europe?
hints: Indonesia is on the other side of the world, in Asia.
No two places on Earth are more than about 20,000 km (12,400 miles) apart.
It's roughly the distance of a flight from New York to Tokyo.
questions.description: You asked for a summer vacation and got a winter, gift-wrapped with a bow.
questions.fun_fact: People called 1816 “the year without a summer”, and the bad weather kept Mary Shelley indoors, where she wrote “Frankenstein”.

questions.question: It's the tiny picture you see before you open a video. YouTubers design it with wild faces and big letters so you click. What is it called?
hints: It's not the channel's profile picture.
Its name is about how small it is.
Its name says it's about as small as a fingernail on your hand.
questions.description: The reason every YouTuber poses with their mouth wide open, as if they'd just seen a ghost.
questions.fun_fact: Long before the internet, artists made quick little drawings called “thumbnail sketches”, because they were barely bigger than a thumbnail.

questions.question: Riddle: I'm a huge frog from North America. I was raised on farms in other countries, escaped, and now I eat the frogs there. What kind of species am I?
hints: It's a problem for the wildlife of the place where it arrived.
It's the opposite of a species native to that place.
It's like someone who walks into a stranger's house and takes over everything.
questions.description: A frog with the appetite of a bull and the manners of a guest nobody invited.
questions.fun_fact: A bullfrog will eat almost anything that fits in its mouth: insects, fish, other frogs, and even small birds!

questions.question: Which animal's name completes both? “___man” (a military diver) and “___ kick” (the leg kick of breaststroke).
hints: It swims by pushing with its back legs.
It lives between water and land.
It croaks in puddles.
questions.description: A question best answered with fins on and a mask pushed up on your forehead.
questions.fun_fact: Modern diving fins were inspired by the webbed feet of frogs and other swimming animals.

questions.question: Look at the photo: in the wild, this black salamander with yellow spots lives in the damp forests of which continent?
hints: It lives on a continent with oak and beech forests.
You can see it in Spain, France and Germany.
It's the continent of medieval castles.
questions.description: An animal dressed up as a bee that never buzzes and never stings.
questions.fun_fact: People once believed this salamander was born from fire, because it came running out of logs thrown onto the fire.

questions.question: A harmless butterfly copies the colors of a bad-tasting one, so birds don't eat it. The trick is named after an English naturalist. What is it called?
hints: The naturalist spent eleven years collecting insects in the Amazon rainforest.
He traveled to the Amazon with Alfred Russel Wallace, but the trick isn't named after Wallace.
His first names were Henry Walter.
questions.description: Nature's most successful Halloween costume is worn all year round.
questions.fun_fact: In the Amazon, Henry Walter Bates collected about 14,700 species, and about 8,000 of them were new to science.

questions.question: In a documentary, a mother pipa toad from the Amazon has dozens of eggs sunk into the skin of her back. What comes out of those holes months later?
wrong_answers: Eggs that drop into the water
hints: They skip a stage that almost all frogs spend swimming freely.
The whole transformation happens inside the mother's skin.
They come out ready to live like tiny adults.
questions.description: A mom who literally carries her kids on her back… on the inside.
questions.fun_fact: The pipa toad is so flat that it looks like a dead leaf floating in the water.

questions.question: Roughly how wide is a great egret from wingtip to wingtip with its wings spread?
hints: It's a big bird, but it's no condor.
With its wings open, it would be almost as wide as an adult is tall.
A little less than the length of a bed.
questions.description: A bird so elegant it always looks dressed for a wedding.
questions.fun_fact: In the early 1900s, so many egrets were hunted for hat feathers that they almost disappeared, which led to new laws to protect them.

questions.question: Ana checks every comma in her report but forgets the conclusion; Luis compares 30 paint colors and misses the leaking roof. Which saying fits them?
questions.answer: Can't see the forest for the trees
wrong_answers: As the twig is bent, so grows the tree
The apple doesn't fall far from the tree
Great oaks from little acorns grow
hints: They focus so hard on the details that they miss something important.
They need to step back and look at the whole picture.
The saying talks about lots of trees together.
questions.description: For people who grab a magnifying glass when they really need binoculars.
questions.fun_fact: Spanish has almost the same saying: “los árboles no dejan ver el bosque”, meaning “the trees don't let you see the forest”.

questions.question: This headless Greek statue with huge wings stands at the top of a staircase in the Louvre. Which goddess does it show?
hints: She was a goddess who showed up whenever someone won a battle.
The statue was set on the front of a ship made of stone.
A famous sports shoe brand is named after her.
questions.description: A statue that lost its head but never lost its style.
questions.fun_fact: The statue was found in 1863 on the Greek island of Samothrace, broken into more than a hundred pieces.

questions.question: It's round, it arranges colors like a rainbow biting its own tail, and the colors facing each other on it are called complementary. What is it?
hints: Painters and designers use it to match colors.
On it, red sits opposite green.
It is also called a “chromatic circle”, from the Greek word “chroma”, meaning color.
questions.description: It goes round and round, but it will never take you anywhere.
questions.fun_fact: Isaac Newton was one of the first people to draw the colors in a circle, in 1704.

questions.question: Which style do the Paris metro entrances with iron stems, Alfons Mucha's posters and Victor Horta's curvy houses share?
hints: It was in fashion around the year 1900.
It loves curvy lines inspired by nature.
Its French name means “new art”.
questions.description: A style that loved plants but never watered a single one.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain this style was called modernismo, and Gaudí is its most famous architect.

questions.question: What do the flags of Mali, Ghana and Ethiopia have in common?
questions.answer: They use green, yellow and red
wrong_answers: They use red, white and blue
They use black, red and gold
They use green, white and orange
hints: All three countries are in Africa.
These colors are known as “Pan-African” colors.
The same three colors appear on a traffic light.
questions.description: Three flags that showed up in matching outfits without sending each other a single text.
questions.fun_fact: The Pan-African colors were inspired by the flag of Ethiopia, one of the few African countries that was never a colony.

questions.question: The outline of this island appears on its country's flag. Which country is it?
hints: It lies in the Mediterranean Sea, near Turkey.
In Greek mythology, Aphrodite was born there.
The Latin word for “copper” comes from this island's name.
questions.description: A country so proud of its figure that it put a self-portrait on its flag.
questions.fun_fact: Cyprus and Kosovo are the only countries with a map of their land drawn on their flag.

questions.question: This curved tool with a handle was used to cut wheat and grass. It appears crossed with a hammer on the red flag of the Soviet Union. What tool is it?
hints: My blade is shaped like a half moon.
I stand for the farmers, and the hammer stands for the factory workers.
My name has six letters and rhymes with “pickle”.
questions.description: A farm tool that ended up with a place of honor on a flag.
questions.fun_fact: The Soviet flag was used until 1991, when the country split into 15 republics.

questions.question: In what year did the Endurance, Ernest Shackleton's ship, set sail for Antarctica?
hints: It was early in the 20th century.
It was the same year a great war broke out in Europe.
The First World War was just beginning.
questions.description: A ship named after the very thing it would need most.
questions.fun_fact: The wreck of the Endurance was found in 2022, almost 3,000 m (nearly 10,000 ft) down, so well preserved that you could still read its name on the stern.

questions.question: My name reads the same forwards and backwards, and from high on the ship I spot other ships in thick fog. What do I “see” them with?
hints: I work even at night or in fog.
I send out invisible waves and listen for the echo.
My name starts with the same two letters as a device that plays music.
questions.description: A gadget with a name that reads both ways and eyes that aren't really eyes.
questions.fun_fact: “Radar” is short for “RAdio Detection And Ranging”: finding things and measuring their distance by radio.

questions.question: I'm a ship, and the captain shouts: “We've run aground!” What happened to me?
questions.answer: I got stuck on sand or rocks
wrong_answers: My sails ran out of wind
I got tied up at the dock
hints: It happens where the water is shallow.
My hull touched the bottom.
I can't move anymore because I'm stuck down below.
questions.description: When a ship decides to settle down somewhere it really shouldn't.
questions.fun_fact: In 2021 the giant ship Ever Given ran aground in the Suez Canal and blocked it for about six days.

questions.question: Bushido, “the way of the warrior”, was a code of honor that also valued the tea ceremony. Which country does it come from?
hints: It’s an island country in Asia.
The warriors who followed it carried katanas.
It’s the land of the samurai.
questions.description: A book of good manners for people who walked around with very sharp swords.
questions.fun_fact: The word “bushido” became famous around the world thanks to an English-language book from 1900 by Inazō Nitobe.

questions.question: Which of these cities is the capital of its country?
hints: It is a planned city, built almost from scratch.
It replaced Lagos as the capital in 1991.
It is in Nigeria.
questions.description: This influencer's GPS badly needs an update.
questions.fun_fact: Nigeria moved its capital to Abuja partly because it is closer to the center of the country than Lagos.

questions.question: What do Asunción, Vienna and Kabul have in common?
questions.answer: They are capitals of landlocked countries
wrong_answers: They are capitals on the Danube River
They are capitals in the Southern Hemisphere
They are capitals over 3,000 m (9,800 ft) high
hints: Look at the map, not at history.
Think of Paraguay, Austria and Afghanistan.
From none of these countries can you reach a beach without crossing a border.
questions.description: Three cities that have nothing in common… or almost nothing.
questions.fun_fact: Paraguay and Bolivia are the only countries in South America with no coastline.

questions.question: What is the final step of 3D animation, where the computer works out light, shadows and textures to make the finished image?
hints: It happens at the very end, after the characters are built and moved.
Pixar films need whole farms of computers to do it.
Architects use the same word for a realistic finished picture of a building that isn't built yet.
questions.description: The computer thinks about this one so long you have time to make yourself a coffee.
questions.fun_fact: In Pixar's early films, some frames took hours to render, and a single film has more than 100,000 frames.

questions.question: What do the zoetrope, the thaumatrope and the praxinoscope, all 19th-century inventions, have in common?
questions.answer: They create an illusion of motion
hints: They were popular toys long before television existed.
They use drawings that change just a tiny bit from one to the next.
Spin them fast enough and the drawings seem to come to life.
questions.description: The great-grandparents of the movies, from back when cinema couldn't even crawl yet.
questions.fun_fact: The word “zoetrope” comes from Greek and means something like “wheel of life.”

questions.question: I hang up at birthday parties, and blindfolded kids hit me with a stick. When I break, what falls out of me?
hints: Every kid loves what falls out.
Everyone dives to the floor to grab it fast.
Think lollipops, gummies and chocolates.
questions.description: The only party guest everyone wants to hit, and it's thrilled about it.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, the traditional piñata is shaped like a star with seven points.

questions.question: The Golden Bear is the top prize of the Berlin film festival. Which of these is NOT a film festival prize?
hints: Three of them are handed out in Venice, Cannes and San Sebastián.
The impostor is won with goals, not with films.
It goes to the top goal scorer in Europe's national leagues.
questions.description: A red carpet full of golden trophies, and one of them sneaked in without an invitation.
questions.fun_fact: The prize is a bear because the bear is the symbol of Berlin and appears on the city's coat of arms.

questions.question: With spaghetti and just three more things, garlic, olive oil and chili pepper, you make a famous Italian pasta. What is it called?
hints: It's a very cheap dish that Italians cook at midnight.
Its full Italian name lists its ingredients.
Its name is Italian for “garlic and oil.”
questions.description: The perfect recipe for when the fridge is empty and the pantry almost is too.
questions.fun_fact: In the movie “Chef” (2014), the main character cooks this dish for Scarlett Johansson in a famous scene.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this Japanese sweet is the favorite food of a famous cartoon character. Whose?
hints: This character comes from the future.
It has a magic pocket full of gadgets.
It's a blue robot cat with no ears.
questions.description: Two pancakes in a tight hug, with something sweet squeezed in between.
questions.fun_fact: The filling of a dorayaki is a sweet red bean paste called “anko.”

questions.question: This Mexican state on the Gulf coast gave the world the song “La Bamba” and a famous fish dish with tomatoes, olives and capers. Which state is it?
hints: It has one of Mexico's most important ports.
The red snapper dish is called “huachinango a la…”
Its name means “true cross” in Spanish.
questions.description: A place with so much rhythm that even its fish can dance.
questions.fun_fact: Many European spices and ingredients, like olives and capers, first reached Mexico through its port.

questions.question: On a cold morning in Mexico, you're served a hot, thick drink of corn dough, chocolate and piloncillo. What is it called?
hints: It's a type of atole, a traditional hot corn drink.
It's often served with tamales on the Day of the Dead and at Christmas.
Its name comes from the Spanish verb “champurrar”, to mix.
questions.description: A drink so thick you could almost eat it with a spoon.
questions.fun_fact: It's frothed with a wooden whisk called a molinillo, spun between the palms of the hands.

questions.question: It protects places like Machu Picchu and Cartagena, and living traditions too. In 2010 it added traditional Mexican cuisine to its list. Which organization is it?
hints: It is part of the United Nations.
It deals with education, science and culture.
It decides what becomes a “World Heritage Site.”
questions.description: An organization that collects treasures… but never locks them in a chest.
questions.fun_fact: In 2010, Mexican cuisine became the first national cuisine on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list, together with the French gastronomic meal.

questions.question: It has a main dish, fries and a drink, you order it by number, and it costs less than buying each item separately. What is it called?
hints: It's the most ordered thing at fast food restaurants.
Its name is short for “combination”.
It starts with “com…”.
questions.description: The math of hunger: burger plus fries plus soda equals… happiness.
questions.fun_fact: At many fast food places, you can “supersize” the fries and drink of your combo by paying just a little more.

questions.question: The sausage dog, long with short legs, comes from which country?
hints: It is a European country famous for its sausages.
The breed's usual name, “dachshund,” means “badger dog” in that country's language.
Its capital is Berlin.
questions.description: A dog shaped like a hot dog bun, or the other way around.
questions.fun_fact: In the United States, hot dogs were first called “dachshund sausages” because they looked like this breed.

questions.question: Complete: “Fries are to potatoes as coleslaw, the shredded salad with mayonnaise, is to…”
hints: It's a vegetable with tightly packed leaves in the shape of a ball.
The “cole” part comes from a Dutch word for this vegetable.
It's a relative of broccoli, and sauerkraut is made from it.
questions.description: A salad whose name sounds like a wizard's spell gone slightly wrong.
questions.fun_fact: “Coleslaw” comes from the Dutch “koolsla”, which means something like “cabbage salad”.

questions.question: A princess is playing by a well when her ball falls into the water, and a frog offers to fetch it if she'll be his friend. What is the ball made of?
hints: It's a toy fit for a princess.
It shines brightly, like a crown.
It's the same material as first-place medals.
questions.description: A princess plays next to a well, and then acts surprised when things go wrong.
questions.fun_fact: In the original Brothers Grimm version, the spell isn't broken by a kiss: the furious princess throws the frog against the wall.

questions.question: “Bicycle” is to “cyclist” as “skateboard” is to…
hints: Think about what you call the person who uses each thing.
The word sounds a lot like the name of the board with wheels.
You'll find lots of them doing tricks on ramps at the skatepark.
questions.description: Four wheels, zero engines and plenty of scraped knees.
questions.fun_fact: Skateboarding made its Olympic debut at the Tokyo 2020 Games.

questions.question: You’re watching a MotoGP race on TV, the fastest motorcycle championship in the world. What do the letters “GP” stand for?
hints: Each race in the championship has this name plus the name of the country.
Formula 1 also uses these words for its races.
The words come from French and mean “big prize”.
questions.description: Two wheels, one engine and a name with mysterious initials.
questions.fun_fact: MotoGP bikes go faster than 350 km/h (about 220 mph) on the longest straights.

questions.question: Tenzing Norgay, who climbed Everest with Hillary, belonged to a people whose name now means Himalayan guide. Which people?
hints: They live in the mountains of Nepal.
Today almost every Everest expedition hires them.
Their name is also used for a jacket with a fluffy lining.
questions.description: A job where the office is on the roof of the world.
questions.fun_fact: On the summit of Everest, Tenzing Norgay left some candy and cookies as an offering, following his Buddhist tradition.

questions.question: Look at the photo: Mongolian nomads in the Gobi Desert live in this round home they can take apart and carry along. What is it called?
hints: It has a wooden frame covered with wool felt.
It isn't the cone-shaped tent of the North American plains peoples.
In Mongolian, it's called a “ger.”
questions.description: A house you can put up, take down and load onto a camel: perfect for escaping unwanted visitors.
questions.fun_fact: A Mongolian family can take down its yurt in one or two hours and load it onto just a few animals.

questions.question: Many African countries are planting a long green wall of trees along the southern edge of the Sahara. What is it for?
questions.answer: To stop the desert from spreading
hints: Its enemy has no weapons: it's the sand.
Plant roots hold the soil so the wind can't blow it away.
Without it, the fertile land would slowly turn into sand.
questions.description: A wall built not with bricks, but with seeds and patience.
questions.fun_fact: The plan for the Great Green Wall is to cross Africa from side to side, from Senegal to Djibouti.

questions.question: It's a natural freshwater pool that forms when the roof of a cave falls in, and Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula has thousands. What is it called?
hints: The Maya used them to get water.
Many people travel to Mexico to swim in them.
The word comes from the Maya word “ts'ono'ot”.
questions.description: A natural swimming pool that made itself when the ground got tired of holding up.
questions.fun_fact: The Maya believed cenotes were doorways to Xibalba, the underworld.

questions.question: Complete: “Argentina is to the 2022 men's World Cup as Spain is to the…”
hints: It's a championship that Spain's women's team won.
It was the biggest title in women's national-team play.
It was played in Australia and New Zealand.
questions.description: An analogy question, so even your English teacher gets to cheer at a match.
questions.fun_fact: The first FIFA Women's World Cup was played in China in 1991, and the United States won it.

questions.question: What do Barcelona's Xavi, Iniesta and Busquets have in common?
hints: All three played in the middle of the field.
They were famous for short passes and almost never losing the ball.
The style's name sounds like the ball going from foot to foot.
questions.description: Three men more in sync than a family group chat planning a birthday surprise.
questions.fun_fact: Spanish TV commentator Andrés Montes made the word “tiki-taka” popular during the 2006 World Cup.

questions.question: Look at this plant: it makes many cats wild with joy. Which plant family does it belong to?
hints: Look at the shape of its leaves, with edges like a saw.
Its cousins are used a lot in cooking and in herbal teas.
If you crush it, it smells a bit like a plant used in chewing gum and mojitos.
questions.description: The only plant that turns a serious cat into a 1970s hippie.
questions.fun_fact: About one in three cats feels nothing at all from catnip: whether a cat reacts to it is inherited.

questions.question: Kittens are born with their eyes closed. About how long does it take them to open them?
hints: It's not a matter of minutes: kittens are born very helpless.
By the time they're running all over the house, they've been able to see for a while.
It's less than a month; a week and a bit.
questions.description: Babies who arrive in the world without reading the instructions on how to open their eyes.
questions.fun_fact: All kittens are born with blue eyes; their final eye color shows up weeks later.

questions.question: People born in this city are nicknamed “gatos” (cats). Look at this detail from one of its most famous statues: which city is it?
hints: It's the capital of a country.
The statue appears on the city's coat of arms.
It stands in the Puerta del Sol, in the capital of Spain.
questions.description: A city where calling someone a “cat” is almost like checking their ID.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says they're called “cats” after a soldier who climbed Madrid's city wall like a cat in the Middle Ages.

questions.question: My name is Muezza. The story goes that I fell asleep on my owner's sleeve, and he cut it off rather than wake me. Who was my owner?
hints: My owner lived on the Arabian Peninsula about 1,400 years ago.
He is a very important religious figure.
He is the prophet of Islam.
questions.description: A cat that slept so sweetly that someone gave up part of his clothes for her.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to stories like this one, cats are much loved in many Muslim countries and are even allowed into mosques.

review.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The question says "The story goes", so the answer Muhammad matches the popular legend, and the wrong answers are wrong. But the story is not in any verified hadith. Scholars say it probably comes from a tale about the saint Ahmad al-Rifa'i (d. 578 AH), and the cat is not named Muezza there. The fun fact about cats being loved and allowed in mosques is broadly true. The hint "He is a very important religious figure" is vague but fine.

questions.question: Who led the roughly fifty Greek heroes who sailed on the ship Argo in search of the Golden Fleece?
hints: He had to bring back the fleece to win back the throne that had been taken from him.
The sorceress Medea helped him.
His sailors are called the Argonauts, “the sailors of the Argo.”
questions.description: A luxury cruise where every passenger is a hero and nobody packed sunscreen.
questions.fun_fact: In some versions of the story, Hercules also sailed on the Argo but was left behind on land halfway through the trip.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this Greek hero, dressed in a lion's skin, had to complete twelve almost impossible labors. Who is he?
hints: He was a son of Zeus.
He was the strongest man in the world.
Disney made a movie about him in 1997.
questions.description: The man with the longest to-do list in all of Greece.
questions.fun_fact: His first labor was to defeat the Nemean lion, and from then on he wore its skin.

questions.question: Listen: this insect sings by stridulation, rubbing one wing against the other. Which insect is it?
hints: You hear it mostly at night, in the grass or in the yard.
It has long back legs for jumping.
In Pinocchio, one of them acts as his conscience.
questions.description: A night-time concert with no tickets, no stage and no permission from the neighbors.
questions.fun_fact: Crickets chirp faster when it's warmer: by counting their chirps, you can estimate the temperature.

questions.question: Wasps build gray nests like this one. What are they made of?
wrong_answers: Wax that comes from their bodies
hints: They get the material by scraping things in the yard.
It looks a lot like paper.
They scrape tree trunks and old fences and chew it up.
questions.description: Builders with no license, no bricks and no cement, and still nobody dares to knock their house down.
questions.fun_fact: In the 18th century, the French scientist Réaumur suggested making paper from wood after watching wasps build their nests.

questions.question: In 1947, fruit flies like this one became the first animals sent into space. Which country launched them?
hints: It wasn't the country of Laika the dog.
They used a V-2 rocket captured after the Second World War.
The launch took place in the New Mexico desert.
questions.description: Before dogs, monkeys and astronauts, space was reached by the little pest that keeps landing on your bananas.
questions.fun_fact: The flies came back alive in a capsule with a parachute, which showed that living things could survive that high up.

questions.question: I'm two letters you see when you write an email, and my name comes from the carbon paper of typewriters. If you put someone in me, what do you do?
questions.answer: Send them a copy everyone can see
hints: My letters are “CC.”
I have a brother, BCC, who does the same thing but in secret.
The two letters stand for “carbon copy.”
questions.description: An invention from the typewriter age that survived into the email era.
questions.fun_fact: With carbon paper, you typed once and got two identical sheets: the original and the copy.

questions.question: I'm the “s” added to the end of “http” in some web addresses. What am I for?
questions.answer: To encrypt data between your browser and the website
wrong_answers: To make the page load faster
To show that the page is a store
To show that the page is from the government
hints: I matter most when you pay by card or type your password.
A little padlock often shows up next to me in the browser.
I turn what you send into a code that nobody can read along the way.
questions.description: One letter worth more than the rest of the alphabet when you pay online.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2018, the Chrome browser has labeled websites that don't use HTTPS as “Not secure”.

questions.question: This word comes from a made-up island in “Gulliver's Travels” whose people are about 15 cm (6 in) tall. Today it means “tiny”. What is it?
hints: When Gulliver reaches the island, he wakes up tied to the ground by a crowd of little people.
The island is at war with its neighbor over which end of an egg you should break.
It describes something very small, like a toy train or a miniature dog.
questions.description: A word so small it fits in a giant's pocket.
questions.fun_fact: In Lilliput, a whole war broke out over whether boiled eggs should be cracked at the big end or the small end.

questions.question: Look at the photo: how many pieces does this cube-shaped puzzle have?
hints: Count slowly, one at a time.
It's more than the fingers on one hand.
It's the same number as the days of the week.
questions.description: A cube that fell to pieces and is waiting for you to put it back together without glue.
questions.fun_fact: Danish inventor Piet Hein created the Soma cube in 1933, and its seven pieces can be put together into a cube in 240 different ways.

questions.question: What is the name of the shape with 20 faces, all of them triangles?
hints: It's a special die, very popular in role-playing games.
Its name comes from Greek and means “twenty faces.”
It starts with “ico.”
questions.description: A shape with so many faces that even the most two-faced person can't compete.
questions.fun_fact: Many viruses, like the adenovirus, have an outer shell shaped like an icosahedron.

questions.question: A hen raises chicks. In “The Wild Robot”, the robot Roz is shipwrecked on an island and raises a baby…
hints: It's a bird that swims in lakes.
It has to learn to fly so it can migrate with its flock.
It's related to the duck, but has a longer neck.
questions.description: The most metal mom in the whole forest.
questions.fun_fact: Peter Brown wrote and illustrated the book, and in 2024 it became an animated DreamWorks movie.

questions.question: In Harry Potter, what does the spell “Wingardium Leviosa!” do?
hints: It's one of the first spells Harry learns in his first year.
In class, they practice it with a feather.
Look at “Leviosa”: it sounds like “levitate”.
questions.description: A spell you have to say just right, or you end up like Ron.
questions.fun_fact: In the movie, Hermione corrects Ron: it's “Levi-O-sa”, not “Levio-SA”.

questions.question: In Harry Potter, what are the Elder Wand, the Resurrection Stone and the Cloak of Invisibility called together?
hints: In a wizard fairy tale, the three Peverell brothers were given these objects.
Their symbol is a triangle with a circle and a line inside it.
The seventh book in the series is named after them.
questions.description: Three gifts so powerful that nobody should ever own all of them, not even your little brother.
questions.fun_fact: Most invisibility cloaks in the wizarding world wear out over time, but Harry's never loses its power.

questions.question: Like corals, some sea animals can bleach because they carry tiny algae inside them. Which of these can NOT bleach?
hints: When they bleach, these animals push out their partner algae, called zooxanthellae.
The ones with these algae often sit in the sun, almost like plants.
It's the only one of the four that spends its day scraping algae off rocks and eating them, instead of carrying them inside.
questions.description: When the reef goes from full rainbow to “blank page” overnight.
questions.fun_fact: A bleached coral isn't dead yet: if the water cools down in time, it can get its algae and its color back.

questions.question: A giant worm with a red plume has no mouth or stomach and lives off the bacteria inside it. Where does it live?
questions.answer: At hydrothermal vents on the seafloor
hints: It lives where sunlight never reaches.
Its bacteria use chemicals instead of light.
It lives next to chimneys that blast very hot water from deep inside the Earth.
questions.description: A worm with no mouth and no stomach that still never orders takeout.
questions.fun_fact: These worms were discovered in 1977 and surprised scientists, who never expected to find so much life without sunlight.

questions.question: I was born in Pisa around 1170. My book “Liber Abaci” helped Europe adopt Arabic numerals and posed a famous puzzle about pairs of rabbits. Who am I?
hints: My real name was Leonardo of Pisa.
I learned math in North Africa, where my dad worked.
A sequence where each number is the sum of the two before it is named after my nickname.
questions.description: A merchant who traveled around the Mediterranean and came home loaded with… numbers.
questions.fun_fact: “Fibonacci” is a nickname meaning “son of Bonacci”; historians gave it to him centuries after his death.

questions.question: Riddle me this: I live inside remote controls and toys and give them power, and when I run out, you shouldn't throw me in the regular trash. What am I?
hints: I come in many sizes: AA, AAA, square ones, and round ones as small as buttons.
When a toy stops turning on, you almost always need to change me.
I have a “+” end and a “−” end.
questions.description: Tiny, full of energy, and with a very delicate ending: just like a five-year-old cousin after a party.
questions.fun_fact: Batteries contain metals like zinc, manganese, and lithium, which can be recovered if you take them to a collection point.

questions.question: Riddle: I spin and spin when water from a dam, steam or wind pushes me, and that turns the generator that makes electricity. What am I?
hints: I don't store energy: I turn it into motion.
I have blades, like a giant fan working in reverse.
Passenger jets carry some on their wings too.
questions.description: Turn this question around a few times and the answer starts to come to you.
questions.fun_fact: The word “turbine” comes from the Latin “turbo”, meaning a whirlwind or something that spins.

questions.question: Look at the photo: why are factory chimneys built so tall?
questions.answer: So the smoke spreads out high above the ground
wrong_answers: So airplanes can see them from far away
So they can store more coal inside
So it rains less on the factory
hints: It has to do with what comes out of the top.
Up there, the wind blows harder than down below.
That way, people living nearby breathe in less smoke directly.
questions.description: Even a factory has to stretch its neck to get a breath of air.
questions.fun_fact: The world's tallest chimney stands at a power plant in Ekibastuz, Kazakhstan, and is about 420 m (1,380 ft) tall.

questions.question: Riddle: I'm a black Night Fury dragon who lost part of my tail. A young Viking built me a new one, and now we fly together. Who is he?
hints: He's the hero of “How to Train Your Dragon”.
He's skinny, loves inventing things, and his dad is the village chief.
His name is what you might get after drinking water too fast.
questions.description: A friendship that started with a direct hit, and not from Cupid's arrow.
questions.fun_fact: Toothless got his name because he can pull his teeth back into his gums, so at first he looks like he has none.

questions.question: This comic strip was created in 1973 by Dik Browne. Its hero is a big-bellied Viking with a horned helmet, and his wife is Helga. What is the strip called?
hints: It ran in the comics section of newspapers.
The hero has a dog named Snert.
The title is the hero's name plus a nickname meaning “terrible”.
questions.description: A Viking who raids castles but is more afraid of his wife.
questions.fun_fact: Real Vikings almost certainly didn't wear horned helmets in battle: that image became popular in the 19th century through operas and paintings.

questions.question: Grauballe Man is a body that the mud of a Danish bog preserved for centuries. What period is he from?
hints: He is much older than he looks, because he is so well preserved.
He lived about 300 years before Christ.
This period is named after a metal that replaced bronze.
questions.description: A man who took a nap in the mud and woke up as a museum piece.
questions.fun_fact: The acidic, oxygen-free water of the bog preserved Grauballe Man so well that you can still see his fingerprints.

questions.question: My pyramid is the second largest at Giza, but it looks the tallest because it stands on higher ground. The Great Sphinx is thought to have my face. Who am I?
hints: My tomb is at Giza, not in the Valley of the Kings.
I was the son of Khufu.
My pyramid still keeps part of its smooth outer casing at the top.
questions.description: A pharaoh who cheated in the tallest-pyramid contest: he built his on a hill.
questions.fun_fact: The Sphinx is about 73 m (240 ft) long and was carved straight out of the bedrock.

questions.question: Look at the stars above the crest on this jersey. What do they count?
questions.answer: The World Cups that team has won
wrong_answers: The famous players on the team
The Copa América titles it won
The times it played in a final
hints: They have nothing to do with the sky.
Brazil has five and Argentina has three.
You earn one by lifting the biggest trophy in soccer.
questions.description: Stars you never see at night, but you see them every time the team walks onto the field.
questions.fun_fact: Argentina added its third star after winning the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

questions.question: I'm a Spanish midfielder: in 2023 I won the World Cup with my national team, was named its best player, then won the Ballon d'Or. Who am I?
hints: I play for Barcelona.
That World Cup was played in Australia and New Zealand.
My first name starts with A, but I'm not Alexia.
questions.description: A player who collects trophies the way other people collect stickers.
questions.fun_fact: With the 2023 title, Spain became the second country, after Germany, to win both the men's and the women's World Cup.

questions.question: An artist taped a fruit to a wall with gray duct tape and called it “Comedian.” Someone paid millions for it… and ate it! What fruit was it?
hints: It's yellow on the outside.
It grows in bunches in tropical places.
You peel it, and it's shaped like a crescent moon.
questions.description: The most expensive work of art that ever ended up as a snack.
questions.fun_fact: In 2024 the artwork sold at auction for more than 6 million dollars, and the banana itself had cost about 35 cents.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is inside these armbands that helps you float?
hints: Before you use them, you have to blow into them.
Birthday balloons have the same thing inside.
If they get a hole, they go flat.
questions.description: The little helpers that hug your arms so you don't sink.
questions.fun_fact: Air weighs much, much less than water, so something full of air pushes upward and helps you float.

questions.question: In what year were the Sydney Olympic Games, where swimmer Eric Moussambani became famous?
hints: They were the last Olympic Games of the 20th century.
Many people remember them as the Games at the turn of the millennium.
The year is a very round number.
questions.description: A swimmer so slow that he became more famous than many champions.
questions.fun_fact: Moussambani swam his heat alone because both of his rivals were disqualified, and the crowd cheered him all the way until he touched the wall.

questions.question: A special family dinner, hugs at midnight and presents under the tree on the night of December 24. What is this night called?
hints: It's the night just before Christmas Day.
It's not the night of December 31.
It's the night when children wait for Santa Claus to bring presents.
questions.description: The only night of the year when the whole family is awake at midnight and nobody gets scolded.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish it's called “Nochebuena”, which means “the good night”.

questions.question: An old atlas says “Macedonia”; a new one says “North Macedonia”. In what year did the official name change?
hints: It happened only a few years ago, not in the last century.
The change came after a deal with Greece, which has a region called Macedonia.
It was just one year before the pandemic began.
questions.description: A country that added a compass direction to its name just to make peace with the neighbors.
questions.fun_fact: The fight with Greece over the name “Macedonia” lasted almost 30 years.

questions.question: I'm a country in Africa, and my name is Ivory Coast. What is the ivory in my name?
hints: It's a creamy white color.
It comes from a very big animal.
That animal has a trunk.
questions.description: A country that sounds like a very fancy beach.
questions.fun_fact: Ivory Coast's national soccer team is nicknamed “The Elephants.”

questions.question: At an arcade machine, you can pick Ryu, Chun-Li or Blanka to fight. What do these three characters have in common?
hints: All three are characters from a very famous fighting game.
That game started out in Capcom's arcade machines.
Its name says the fights happen out on the road, not in a ring.
questions.description: A tournament where nobody showed up to play checkers.
questions.fun_fact: In the game's story, Blanka, the green fighter who shoots out electricity, comes from Brazil.

previous.feedback: The question uses the retired "What do these three characters have in common?" style, which the source also uses. Apart from that, the translation is faithful and natural. The rewritten hint 3 works, and the kept image of a Mazinger Z arcade cabinet fits the question without giving the answer away.

questions.question: My name is course. Pirates set me before they sail, the helmsman keeps me all voyage, and the captain shouts to change me. What do I show?
questions.answer: Which way the ship is sailing
wrong_answers: How fast the ship is going
How much cargo the ship has
How deep the sea is below
hints: A compass helps keep me from getting lost.
Get me wrong and you'll never reach Treasure Island.
North, south, east, west...
questions.description: Without this, a pirate ship is just a floating party with nowhere to go.
questions.fun_fact: When people say their life has gone “off course”, they're using words that were born at sea.

review.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The answer and wrong answers are fine: a ship's course is its heading, not speed, cargo or depth. The fun fact is shaky. "Course" comes from Latin cursus ('a running, path') through Old French cours, so the word was not born at sea. Only the phrase "off course" is plausibly nautical in origin. I did not run searches, so this rests on my own knowledge of the etymology.

questions.question: “Colombia is to country as South America is to…”. Which word completes the sentence?
hints: South America is much bigger than Colombia.
Many countries fit inside South America.
Africa, Europe and Asia are one too.
questions.description: A word puzzle with more ground to cover than a family road trip.
questions.fun_fact: South America has 12 independent countries, and Brazil alone covers almost half of its land.

questions.question: One museum room shows a woolly mammoth, a saber-toothed cat and the first humans. What do they have in common?
questions.answer: They all lived in the Cenozoic Era
wrong_answers: They all lived in the Mesozoic Era
They all lived in the Paleozoic Era
They all lived in the Precambrian
hints: None of them shared the planet with a T. rex.
It is the era we are living in right now.
It began just after the big dinosaurs died out.
questions.description: A museum room with more hair than a prehistoric barbershop.
questions.fun_fact: “Cenozoic” comes from Greek and means “new life.”

questions.question: Megalodon left behind almost nothing but fossil teeth like this one, because its skeleton was made of a material that rarely fossilizes. Which one?
hints: Today's sharks have skeletons made of the same material.
It is softer and bendier than bone.
You have it in the tip of your nose and in your ears.
questions.description: A shark so big the tooth fairy would need a truck.
questions.fun_fact: The biggest megalodon teeth are over 15 cm (6 in) long, bigger than a child's hand.

questions.question: The air plant hangs from branches and even power lines, needs no soil, and its leaves are covered in silvery scales. What are those scales for?
questions.answer: To catch water and food from the air
hints: Its roots are used almost only for holding on.
It has to get what other plants take from the soil from somewhere else.
They work like sponges when it rains or when there is fog.
questions.description: The laziest plant in the world: it doesn't even bother to get a pot.
questions.fun_fact: The air plant is a relative of the pineapple: both are bromeliads.

questions.question: Riddle: I live inside a frozen mountain on a Norwegian island near the North Pole, and people call me the “Doomsday Vault”. What do I keep?
questions.answer: Crop seeds from around the world
wrong_answers: Gold bars for the world's reserves
hints: What I keep could help the world start over after a huge disaster.
Almost every country in the world has sent me something to keep safe.
If you opened me, you would find beans, rice, corn and wheat… uncooked and ready to plant.
questions.description: A place so cold and so hidden that not even the bravest delivery driver dares to go there.
questions.fun_fact: The vault is in Svalbard because the cold of the permafrost would keep the seeds frozen even if the power went out.

questions.question: The real flowers of the bougainvillea are tiny and white. So what makes it look so colorful?
wrong_answers: A fungus that dyes its branches
hints: It isn't part of the flower, even though it's attached to it.
Botanists call them “bracts.”
It's the same plant part that does photosynthesis, just in a different color.
questions.description: A plant that dresses up for a party but hides its real face.
questions.fun_fact: The poinsettia, the famous Christmas flower, pulls the same trick: its red “flower” is also made of modified leaves.

questions.question: In biology class, you take apart a lily flower and separate the stigma, the style and the ovary. Which part of the flower are all three pieces of?
hints: It is the female part of the flower.
It usually sits right in the center of the flower.
Pollen lands there, and that is where the seeds form.
questions.description: The part of the flower where everything starts turning into fruit.
questions.fun_fact: The red threads of saffron, one of the most expensive spices in the world, are the stigmas of a flower.

questions.question: Riddle: “I am the manguaré, the great drum of the Bora people; when struck, my voice carries messages for kilometers through the jungle.” What am I made of?
hints: My material comes straight from the jungle, and it's very heavy.
I have no animal skin that vibrates.
A whole tree, emptied out on the inside.
questions.description: The jungle's group chat: no Wi-Fi, but plenty of rhythm.
questions.fun_fact: Manguarés are played in pairs: a “male” one and a “female” one, each with its own sound.

questions.question: According to a famous legend of the South American rainforest, what is Paititi?
questions.answer: A lost city of the Incas
wrong_answers: A sunken galleon full of treasure
hints: It is said to be hidden in the jungle where Peru, Bolivia and Brazil meet.
People say it had streets, palaces and lots of people living there.
It's a “cousin” of the legend of El Dorado.
questions.description: A name that sounds like baby talk, but hides a giant legend.
questions.fun_fact: According to the legend, the Incas hid their treasures there so the Spanish conquerors couldn't find them.

questions.question: What is the main component of the gas that is collected from landfills and burned to make electricity?
hints: Microbes make it when they break down garbage without air.
Cows also let it out when they burp.
It is the main component of the natural gas used in kitchen stoves.
questions.description: Garbage passes gas too, and someone had the bright idea to put it to work.
questions.fun_fact: Landfill biogas is roughly half methane and half carbon dioxide.

questions.question: You want to buy cheap used clothes. Which of these places is NOT a typical place to find them?
hints: Think carefully about what each word means.
One of these places sells new things for sewing.
It's where you buy buttons, thread and zippers.
questions.description: Your favorite jacket had a whole other life before it met you.
questions.fun_fact: The name “flea market” comes from the French “marché aux puces”, because the old clothes sold in Paris markets were said to have fleas.

questions.question: Each green dot in this photo is a complete living thing, smaller than a grain of rice. Which group does it belong to?
hints: They make food from sunlight, like the grass in the park.
Hard to believe, but they are distant relatives of roses and sunflowers.
It's the smallest in the world of all those that can bloom.
questions.description: Blink and you'll miss a whole garden.
questions.fun_fact: Wolffia is the smallest flowering plant in the world: its flowers are so tiny you can barely see them with the naked eye.

questions.question: What do Mount Everest, Aconcagua and Mount Vinson have in common?
questions.answer: Each is its continent's highest peak
wrong_answers: Each is in the Andes mountains
Each is in the Himalaya mountains
hints: They are on different continents.
Mount Vinson is in Antarctica.
Aconcagua holds that same title in the Americas.
questions.description: A to-do list for climbers with way too much vacation time.
questions.fun_fact: Mount Vinson, about 4,892 m (16,050 ft) tall, is so remote in Antarctica that nobody climbed it until 1966.

questions.question: I'm a pine tree in the mountains of California, over 4,800 years old. I'm named after a Bible figure famous for living 969 years. Who is he?
hints: He was the grandfather of someone famous for building an ark.
People say someone is “as old as…” him when they mean very, very old.
His name starts with M.
questions.description: A tree so old its birthday cake would need a whole forest of candles.
questions.fun_fact: The exact location of the Methuselah tree is kept secret to protect it from visitors who might want to take home a souvenir.

questions.question: How many chambers (atria and ventricles) does a frog's heart have in total?
hints: It has fewer chambers than a human heart.
In this, amphibians are halfway between fish and mammals.
It's an odd number: two atria and just one ventricle.
questions.description: An organ that works day and night without a vacation, even if its owner lives in a puddle.
questions.fun_fact: Because its heart mixes the blood a little, a frog gets extra help by also breathing through its moist skin.

questions.question: Complete: the elephant is to its trunk as the giant anteater is to its…
hints: It pokes its snout into ant and termite nests.
It doesn't have a single tooth.
It's long and sticky, and it flicks in and out super fast.
questions.description: An animal whose whole menu is right there in its name.
questions.fun_fact: A giant anteater's tongue is about 60 cm (2 ft) long and can flick in and out about 150 times a minute.

questions.question: Riddle: I'm a mangrove root, but I don't dig down. I poke up out of the mud like a pencil, and the tide covers and uncovers me. What am I for?
questions.answer: Taking in oxygen from the air
hints: I do most of my work when the tide goes out.
There's almost no oxygen in mangrove mud.
I work like a diver's snorkel.
questions.description: A tree standing with its feet in salty mud came up with a clever trick.
questions.fun_fact: These roots are called pneumatophores, from Greek words meaning “air carriers”.

questions.question: In Collodi's book “Pinocchio”, a coachman sells donkeys at the market. What were those donkeys before?
questions.answer: Boys who didn't want to study
hints: The same thing happens to Pinocchio himself.
Before they had long ears, they spent all day playing.
The coachman took them to a place with no school and no teachers.
questions.description: A trip that's pure fun from start to finish, until it ends in a hee-haw.
questions.fun_fact: In the Disney film that place became an island, but in the book it's a land the children reach in a cart pulled by little donkeys.

questions.question: Riddle: I'm the largest continuous sea of sand in the world, I cover the south of the Arabian Peninsula, and my name means “the empty quarter.” Who am I?
hints: Saudi Arabia, Oman, Yemen and the United Arab Emirates share my land.
My dunes can be more than 200 m (650 ft) tall.
My name is in Arabic and starts with “Rub.”
questions.description: A desert named after a room nobody ever wants to clean.
questions.fun_fact: Beneath its sands lies Shaybah, one of Saudi Arabia's great oil fields.

questions.question: The oilbird nests in pitch-dark caves and flies between the rocks without crashing. How does it find its way?
questions.answer: With the echo of its own sounds
wrong_answers: With the heat of the rocks
hints: It's about how they find their way without seeing anything.
They make sounds and listen to what comes back.
It's called echolocation.
questions.description: A place so dark that not even a lamp would help you find the way out.
questions.fun_fact: The oilbird is the only flying bird that feeds on fruit at night, and Alexander von Humboldt studied it in 1799 in the Cueva del Guácharo in Venezuela.

questions.question: Benjamin Franklin, the man with the famous kite in the storm, invented three of these things. Which one did he NOT invent?
hints: One of his inventions came straight from his kite experiment.
The one that isn't his came more than a hundred years later.
That one is mostly credited to Thomas Edison.
questions.description: A man who flew kites in the middle of a storm… and no, don't try this at home.
questions.fun_fact: Franklin never patented his inventions: he wanted everyone to be able to use them for free.

questions.question: What do a cat, an owl and a crocodile have in common?
wrong_answers: They see in black and white
hints: It has to do with how they protect their eyes.
It's a thin film that slides sideways across the eye.
On top of the usual two, they have one more.
questions.description: A cat, an owl and a crocodile walk into a doctor's office… and no, this isn't the start of a joke.
questions.fun_fact: You can sometimes see a cat's third eyelid when it's half asleep or sick: it's a thin white film in the corner of the eye.

questions.question: Daedalus designed it, it was on Crete, and Theseus got out of it by following Ariadne's thread. What was it?
hints: A monster was locked up inside it.
That monster was half man, half bull.
It is full of corridors and dead ends.
questions.description: A job for a king with more secrets than Grandma's junk room.
questions.fun_fact: The English word “clue” comes from “clew,” an old word for a ball of thread, like the one Ariadne gave Theseus.

questions.question: A kitchen knife is to a Swiss Army knife as an AI that can only play chess is to…
hints: The Swiss Army knife isn't bigger: it can do more things.
Scientists haven't managed to actually build it yet.
Its short name is AGI, and it's the opposite of a “narrow” or specialized AI.
questions.description: Machines have their own “when I grow up, I want to be…” too.
questions.fun_fact: Several AI labs, such as OpenAI, openly say that building artificial general intelligence is their main goal.

questions.question: Copilot is made by Microsoft and shows up in Windows, Word and Excel with a colorful icon. Its name comes from the person who sits next to the pilot. What is Copilot?
questions.answer: An assistant that answers your questions
wrong_answers: A checker that underlines your mistakes
A guard that blocks computer viruses
A search tool that finds your files
hints: It has nothing to do with planes, even if the name sounds like it.
You can ask it to sum up a document or help you write an email.
It's a chatbot, from the same family as ChatGPT.
questions.description: Someone has to sit next to the pilot, and it isn't always a person.
questions.fun_fact: Before it came to Windows, the name was used for GitHub Copilot, launched in 2021 to help programmers write code.

questions.question: It started in 2013 as a joke, its symbol is the Shiba Inu dog from the Doge meme, and Elon Musk has posted about it many times. What is it?
hints: Some people buy and sell it.
It doesn't exist as paper bills or metal coins.
It's a relative of Bitcoin.
questions.description: Such doggo. Very internet. Wow.
questions.fun_fact: The dog in the meme was named Kabosu and lived in Japan with her owner, a teacher.

questions.question: The name of the Canary Islands comes from Latin and hides an animal. Which one?
hints: The Romans already knew about these islands in the Atlantic.
In Latin, this animal was called “canis.”
It's the animal that wags its tail when you come home.
questions.description: A name that looks obvious, but has hidden a surprise since Roman times.
questions.fun_fact: It's the other way around from what most people think: the canary bird is named after the islands, not the islands after the bird.

questions.question: What do Hong Kong, Singapore and Jamaica have in common in their history?
hints: That European empire left all three its language as an official language.
That empire had the most powerful navy in the world in the 19th century.
In all three places, people still drive on the left.
questions.description: Three places with beaches, lots of heat and a past that arrived by ship from Europe.
questions.fun_fact: Hong Kong was handed back to China in 1997, after more than 150 years under British rule.

questions.question: In the film “My Neighbor Totoro,” how many Totoros appear?
hints: He is not alone in the forest.
They are not all the same size: the biggest one is the one waiting for the bus in the rain.
It's the same number as the little pigs in the story with the big bad wolf.
questions.description: The giant cuddly toy everyone would love as a pillow on a rainy day.
questions.fun_fact: Totoro appears in the logo of Studio Ghibli, the Japanese studio that made the film in 1988.

questions.question: García Márquez is to “One Hundred Years of Solitude” as Isabel Allende is to…
hints: It is Isabel Allende's first novel, from 1982.
It tells the story of several generations of the Trueba family.
Its title is about a home full of ghosts.
questions.description: A question for people who read long novels with even longer family trees.
questions.fun_fact: “The House of the Spirits” began as a letter Isabel Allende started writing to her grandfather in 1981.

questions.question: In “Love in the Time of Cholera”, Florentino Ariza waits and waits for his love, Fermina Daza. How many years does he wait, according to the novel?
hints: It's a very long time: when they finally get together, they are both old.
The novel says: “… years, nine months and four days.”
It's a number just over 50.
questions.description: The longest wait in literature, worse than the line at the bank on a Monday.
questions.fun_fact: García Márquez based this novel partly on the love story of his own parents.

questions.question: I'm the Minecraft enchanting table: I have a book that floats and opens when you come close. What happens if you surround me with bookshelves?
wrong_answers: You can enchant several items at once
You no longer need lapis lazuli
hints: The bookshelves must be nearby, but with one free block between them and the table.
Look at the numbers next to each enchantment option.
More books around it, more magical wisdom for the table.
questions.description: A piece of furniture that reads more than you do, and it doesn't even have eyes.
questions.fun_fact: With enough bookshelves around it, the Minecraft enchanting table can offer level 30 enchantments.

questions.question: On a day trip, you drink tap water, swim in a river and later row on a mountain lake. What do those three waters have in common?
hints: None of them tastes like the sea.
It's the kind people and animals can drink.
Its name uses the same word as bread just out of the oven.
questions.description: A day out in the country with three different dips and not a single wave.
questions.fun_fact: Almost all the water on Earth is salty: fresh water is only about 3%, and most of it is frozen.

previous.feedback: The question asks what three given things have in common (“What do those three waters have in common?”). That style is retired (reason 7), and it applies to the source too. The translation itself is faithful, and the new hint 3 (fresh bread) works well in English.

questions.question: He's called the father of geometry, wrote a book called “Elements” and lived about 2,300 years ago. Which civilization was Euclid from?
hints: His civilization was famous for its philosophers.
He came from the same culture as Pythagoras and Archimedes.
His civilization also invented the Olympic Games.
questions.description: The man who turned triangles into a bestseller for more than 2,000 years.
questions.fun_fact: Euclid's “Elements” is one of the most-printed books in history and was used in schools for more than 2,000 years.

questions.question: This lump of corroded bronze was pulled from a Greek shipwreck in 1901. What was the Antikythera mechanism used for?
questions.answer: Predicting eclipses and movements in the sky
wrong_answers: Measuring how deep the sea is
hints: It had dozens of gear wheels, like a clock.
It showed the Sun, the Moon and maybe some planets.
It is seen as the oldest known astronomical calculator.
questions.description: Divers looking for sea sponges found a 2,000-year-old bronze puzzle on the seabed.
questions.fun_fact: Nobody built a device with such complex gears again until the astronomical clocks of the Middle Ages, more than a thousand years later.

questions.question: Which of these energy sources is NOT renewable?
hints: Renewable sources never run out: they come back on their own.
The one you want is dug out of a mine, like a rock.
It's used in nuclear power plants, like the one where Homer Simpson works.
questions.description: Some energy comes back by itself every day, and some is gone for good once it runs out.
questions.fun_fact: One uranium fuel pellet, about the size of a fingertip, gives as much energy as a ton of coal.

questions.question: Riddle: I am Brísingamen, the golden necklace of the goddess Freya. Four brothers in Norse myth forged me. What kind of beings were they?
hints: In Norse myths, these beings also made famous weapons for the gods.
They live underground and are the best blacksmiths.
They are small, bearded and work in mines.
questions.description: The shiniest jewel in Asgard, and nobody bought it at the mall.
questions.fun_fact: In the myths, dwarves also forged Mjölnir, Thor's hammer.

questions.question: What is an oath, like the one some people make to their flag?
hints: It is said out loud and with great respect.
Whoever makes it commits to doing something.
It's like saying “I promise”, but in a very serious way.
questions.description: When school asks you to be really serious, at least for a little while.
questions.fun_fact: In many Latin American countries, children make their oath to the flag at a special school ceremony.

questions.question: The ancient Egyptians painted this eye on their boats and wore it around their necks. What did they use it for?
questions.answer: To protect themselves and stay healthy
wrong_answers: To guide their boats along the Nile
To show that they were nobles
To measure the passing of time
hints: Both rich and poor people used it.
The living wore it, and it was also placed on mummies.
According to the myth, the falcon god's eye was healed after a fight.
questions.description: An eye that has been watching for thousands of years and still doesn't need glasses.
questions.fun_fact: The Eye of Horus is still worn today as a pendant on necklaces and shows up in many video games.

questions.question: The “Mona Lisa” is to the Louvre as which painting is to the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam?
hints: It was painted by the same artist the museum is named after.
It shows yellow flowers in a vase.
These flowers turn their heads to follow the sun.
questions.description: A museum for a painter who sold almost nothing while he was alive and is now too famous to fit through the door.
questions.fun_fact: Van Gogh painted several versions of “Sunflowers” to decorate the bedroom of his friend, the painter Paul Gauguin.

questions.question: Turkey is to Christmas dinner in the US as ________ is to Christmas dinner for millions of families in Japan.
hints: You buy it from a famous fast-food chain.
The custom started with an ad campaign in the 1970s.
It comes in buckets, and the brand's founder was a colonel with a white beard.
questions.description: A Christmas tradition that was born in an advertising office.
questions.fun_fact: So many families in Japan order it that they have to reserve their Christmas bucket weeks in advance.

questions.question: Who were the first to come and worship baby Jesus, on the very night he was born?
hints: They were working at night in the fields near Bethlehem.
An angel brought them the news while they watched over their animals.
Their job was looking after sheep.
questions.description: The most exclusive guest list in history, and not a single celebrity on it.
questions.fun_fact: According to the Bible, the Wise Men didn't arrive that night: the Gospel says they found the child in a house.

questions.question: Which ancient people gave Mexico its name and founded their capital where Mexico City stands today?
hints: They ruled central Mexico when the Spanish arrived.
Their capital was called Tenochtitlan and was built on a lake.
They called themselves the “Mexica.”
questions.description: A city so important that it lent its name to the whole country.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico City was built on a lake, so some of its buildings are slowly sinking.

questions.question: Charmander is to Fire type as Lucario is to…
hints: Lucario can sense other creatures' aura, but that's not what decides its type.
Machop and Hitmonchan are this type too.
It's the type of Pokémon that throw punches and kicks.
questions.description: A dog that never barks, but can read everyone's energy.
questions.fun_fact: Lucario actually has two types at once: Fighting and Steel.

questions.question: What links the film “Captain Phillips”, speedboats attacking cargo ships, and warships guarding oil tankers in the Indian Ocean?
hints: It's modern piracy, from this century.
It happens near the entrance to the Red Sea.
These pirates come from the country whose capital is Mogadishu.
questions.description: Pirates with no parrot and no wooden leg, but with very fast boats.
questions.fun_fact: “Captain Phillips” is based on the real hijacking of the cargo ship Maersk Alabama in 2009.

previous.feedback: The question asks what several given things have in common ("What links the film “Captain Phillips”, speedboats… and warships…?"). That is the retired "what do they have in common" style. The source uses the same style ("¿Qué tienen en común…?"), so the source has the same problem.

questions.question: They call me hardtack, and I turn up in lots of pirate stories. Sailors soaked me before biting, and I lasted months in the hold. What am I?
wrong_answers: A sponge cake of egg and sugar
An oat cake made with honey
hints: Sailors sometimes found weevils living inside me.
I was baked several times to dry out every bit of moisture.
I'm made of just flour, water and salt.
questions.description: The pirates' favorite snack, if you don't care about your teeth.
questions.fun_fact: Some pieces of hardtack more than 150 years old are still kept in museums.

questions.question: I'm the Amazon River: in the rainy season I rise several meters and spill into the rainforest. What happens then?
wrong_answers: Pink river dolphins leave for the sea
Monkeys move down to live on the ground
hints: For months, the forest is half underwater.
Down there, visitors with fins start showing up.
Some of them eat the fruit that falls from the branches.
questions.description: A river that leaves home every year without asking permission.
questions.fun_fact: Some Amazon fish eat fruit and drop the seeds far away, so they help plant the rainforest.

questions.question: A giant tree trunk is hollowed out with fire and an ax, and left long and pointed at both ends. What is it used for?
hints: The pointed ends help it cut through something that moves.
In the rainforest, rivers are like roads.
It's going to need some paddles.
questions.description: A tree that got hollowed out and found itself a whole new career.
questions.fun_fact: Some canoes carved from a single tree trunk can carry more than ten people.

questions.question: At a school fair, one ticket buys one cupcake. In the carbon credit market, one credit stands for… what?
questions.answer: One metric ton of CO₂ kept out of the air
wrong_answers: One kilogram of CO₂ kept out of the air
One liter of CO₂ kept out of the air
100 metric tons of CO₂ kept out of the air
hints: It's an amount of greenhouse gas.
It's a fairly big unit, not one you'd use on a kitchen scale.
It's a thousand kilograms of carbon dioxide.
questions.description: Polluting with permission: the grown-up version of “I'll trade you my dessert for your homework.”
questions.fun_fact: Carbon credits became famous with the Kyoto Protocol, adopted in Japan in 1997.

questions.question: Monarch butterflies fly from Canada and the United States to spend the winter in mountain forests. In which country are they?
hints: Spanish is spoken in this country.
The butterflies never cross the equator.
It's the country of mariachis and tacos.
questions.description: Travelers who need no passport, just a pair of colorful wings.
questions.fun_fact: No single monarch butterfly makes the whole round trip: its great-grandchildren finish the journey back north.

questions.question: On which day is the crown-shaped sweet bread with candied fruit and a hidden surprise inside traditionally eaten?
hints: By that day, Christmas and New Year's are already over.
Its crown shape is a clue about who is celebrated that day.
It's the day of Melchior, Caspar and Balthazar.
questions.description: A bread with a prize inside, like cereal boxes used to have.
questions.fun_fact: A tiny baby Jesus figure is hidden inside the bread, and in Mexico whoever finds it must treat everyone to tamales on February 2.

questions.question: iCub is a robot the size of a small child, built at an institute in Genoa. Which Italian scientist co-led its development?
hints: He has worked in Genoa for most of his career.
He became scientific director of the Italian Institute of Technology.
His first name is the Italian form of “George”.
questions.description: A baby that never cries, never sleeps and comes with an instruction manual anyone can read.
questions.fun_fact: Dozens of iCub copies are spread across labs around the world, and they all share their design freely.

questions.question: I'm the name of the horsemen of the steppes of Ukraine and southern Russia, and I come from a Turkic word. What did my name, “Cossack”, first mean?
hints: The same word gave its name to a country in Central Asia.
