His brothers fall in love with Jimena and Sara.
He is played by the actor Mario Cimarro.
questions.description: Three brothers, three sisters and more drama than a Sunday family lunch.
questions.fun_fact: “Pasión de gavilanes” is a remake of “Las aguas mansas,” another Colombian telenovela written by Julio Jiménez.

questions.question: “Pablito clavó un clavito: ¿qué clavito clavó Pablito?” What kind of phrase is this?
hints: There’s no answer to guess.
The fun is saying it very fast without slipping up.
Say it five times quickly and your mouth starts tripping over itself.
questions.description: Pablito has been hammering away at this one since your grandparents were in school.
questions.fun_fact: Tongue twisters exist in almost every language and are used to practice pronunciation.

questions.question: Tío Conejo tricks bigger, fiercer animals, and Pedro Rimales makes fun of the king, though neither is strong. What quality makes them win?
hints: It has to do with the head, not the body.
A fox is the classic symbol of this quality.
It means being sharp and quick-witted, always one step ahead.
questions.description: The superpower of those with no muscles but plenty of brains.
questions.fun_fact: Pedro Rimales is a cousin of the rogues in Spanish folk tales, who also won with tricks rather than strength.

questions.question: Look at this rock carved with channels and figures in the San Agustín Archaeological Park. What is it called?
hints: Water runs through channels carved in the stone.
It has carved snakes, lizards and people.
In Spanish, its name sounds like a place where you'd wash your feet.
questions.description: A water park more than a thousand years old: no slides, but plenty of snakes.
questions.fun_fact: The Fuente de Lavapatas is thought to have been a place for water rituals, and it has been part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995.

questions.question: How does the saying “ojos que no ven…” (eyes that don't see…) end?
hints: It's about not suffering over what you don't know.
Like the first half, it names a body part, but not one on your face.
It's the organ that beats.
questions.description: The perfect saying for the last arepa that mysteriously vanished.
questions.fun_fact: English has a very similar one: “What the eye doesn't see, the heart doesn't grieve over.”

questions.question: In Cali, Popayán and other Colombian cities, what is “la galería”?
hints: People show up with a bag or a basket.
Vendors shout “¡a la orden!” from their stalls.
It's where people do the week's grocery shopping.
questions.description: A place with a fancy name and an atmosphere that is anything but quiet.
questions.fun_fact: At many market squares in Colombia, you can also have a cheap lunch at the food stalls.

questions.question: Pan tajado comes in a bag, already cut into slices and ready for a sandwich. What flour is it almost always made from?
hints: It's not the same flour you use for arepas.
It comes from a cereal that grows in golden ears.
Almost all pan francés is made with this same flour.
questions.description: Bread that shows up at home with its hair combed, standing in a neat line.
questions.fun_fact: The first machine for slicing bread went on sale in the United States in 1928.

questions.question: Colombian bakeries sell a soft yellow cake in little squares that crumbles easily. It's made with cornstarch, eggs and sugar. What is it called?
hints: You can find it in almost any neighborhood bakery.
It's usually sold in portions wrapped in paper or plastic.
Its name sounds like “manteca”.
questions.description: A ponqué so delicate it falls apart before you've even thought about it.
questions.fun_fact: Mantecada is usually eaten with tinto or hot chocolate at onces, the afternoon snack.

questions.question: Lots of Colombians drop little pieces of something into their hot breakfast aguapanela, and the pieces melt inside. What is it?
hints: It's white.
It's made from milk.
It gets stretchy and melted when you scoop it out with your spoon.
questions.description: A grandma's remedy that cures a cold and a craving at the same time.
questions.fun_fact: Aguapanela is also drunk cold with lime, like a panela lemonade!

questions.question: This is the sacred lake of the Muisca, the one from the El Dorado legend. What do you call someone born in its department?
hints: The lake is Guatavita.
It's the department that surrounds the country's capital.
Its administrative capital is Bogotá.
questions.description: People hunted for gold here for centuries, and the only sure thing that came out was a name for the locals.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says the Muisca chief covered himself in gold dust and bathed in Lake Guatavita as an offering.

questions.question: This bird has a long reddish bill, lives only in the wetlands of the Cundiboyacense highlands and is endangered. Which bird is it?
hints: It hides among the reeds and is hardly ever seen.
It's a relative of moorhens and other rails.
In English it's known as the Bogotá rail.
questions.description: A Bogotá local who'd rather sit in a wetland than in traffic.
questions.fun_fact: The tingua bogotana is endemic to Colombia: it lives in no other country in the world.

questions.question: In Colombia, someone goes up to the finca on a muddy trocha (dirt track) in a campero. What is a campero?
hints: It has an engine and four wheels.
In the Eje Cafetero, people load it with sacks of coffee.
The famous Willys is one of them.
questions.description: It got its name because it loves mud more than pavement.
questions.fun_fact: In Armenia, the Yipao parade shows off Willys camperos loaded with coffee, furniture and even a whole family's move.

questions.question: Who hosts “MasterChef Celebrity Colombia” on Canal RCN?
hints: She started her career as a model before moving into TV.
She earlier hosted “MasterChef Colombia” with contestants who weren't famous.
Her last name starts with “Baha.”
questions.description: In this kitchen, the stars cry more over the judges than over the onions.
questions.fun_fact: The show's judges are chefs Jorge Rausch, Christopher Carpentier and Nicolás de Zubiría.

questions.question: You read “Teresa en cuya frente el cielo empieza” by Eduardo Carranza, leader of the Piedra y Cielo group. In which decade was that group born?
hints: It came before Nadaísmo.
It took its name from a book by Juan Ramón Jiménez.
It published its booklets just as World War II was starting.
questions.description: Poets so lofty they named themselves after something hard and something endless.
questions.fun_fact: The “piedracielistas” published their poems in small booklets meant to shake up Colombian poetry.

questions.question: I was born in Bucaramanga and served as a government minister. My most famous novel tells the life of a German who built trails in Santander in the 19th century. Who am I?
hints: The novel came out in the 1970s.
The German's name was Geo von Lengerke.
The novel is called “La otra raya del tigre.”
questions.description: Some writers look for inspiration in a café; this one found it on a stone trail in the mountains of Santander.
questions.fun_fact: Geo von Lengerke was a real person, and Santander still has hiking trails called the “caminos de Lengerke.”

questions.question: Butterfly houses in Colombia have lots of capsules like this one hanging up. What are they for?
questions.answer: For a caterpillar to turn into a butterfly
wrong_answers: For keeping the butterfly's eggs safe
For the butterfly to sleep in at night
For catching mosquitoes like a trap
hints: Inside, there's an animal that is changing.
Before it went in, that animal crawled around eating leaves.
When it opens, something with colorful wings comes out.
questions.description: Hanging from a leaf, as still as a kid in time-out.
questions.fun_fact: Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar's body breaks down almost completely and rebuilds itself as a butterfly.

questions.question: Hormigas arrieras (leafcutter ants) carry bits of leaf back to their nest. Why?
questions.answer: To grow a fungus that they eat
wrong_answers: To build the roof of the nest
To give shade to their eggs
hints: They can't digest leaves well.
They are farmers, just like people in the countryside.
What they eat grows on the leaves they bring, like mushrooms.
questions.description: The hardest workers in the forest, and they never ask for a Christmas bonus.
questions.fun_fact: The hormigas culonas eaten toasted in Santander are the queens of a kind of leafcutter ant.

questions.question: Look at this wasp. How many legs does it have?
hints: It's an insect, not a spider.
All its legs come out of the middle part of its body.
It has the same number as an ant.
questions.description: It showed up uninvited to the paseo de olla and went straight for the soda.
questions.fun_fact: Only female wasps have a stinger, because it started out as a body part for laying eggs.

questions.question: On that day at church, they put this cross of ash on your forehead. Where does the ash come from?
questions.answer: From burning last year's Palm Sunday fronds
wrong_answers: From burning the Año Viejo effigy
From the candles of Noche de Velitas
hints: It comes from something that was blessed in church.
It's from something used a year earlier.
They're leaves that people wave at church at the start of Holy Week.
questions.description: A little smudge on the forehead that nobody wants to wipe off.
questions.fun_fact: Ash Wednesday starts Lent, about 40 days before Holy Week.

questions.question: I was brought to Cartagena in chains, but one day I escaped into the hills. With others like me, I built a free palenque. Who am I?
hints: I was enslaved.
Benkos Biohó was one of us.
My name was also used for farm animals that went wild.
questions.description: A figure from colonial Cartagena who never showed up in the viceroys' portraits.
questions.fun_fact: San Basilio de Palenque, founded by cimarrones, is considered the first free town in the Americas.

questions.question: Look at the photo: Lucho Herrera and Nairo Quintana won this red polka-dot jersey at the Tour de France. Who wears it?
hints: You don't win it on the flat finishes.
Riders earn points by getting to certain spots first.
Those points are handed out at the top of mountain passes.
questions.description: A jersey that looks like it came from one of grandma's dresses, but every escarabajo dreams of wearing it.
questions.fun_fact: Lucho Herrera won the Tour's mountains jersey twice, in 1985 and 1987.

questions.question: A Colombian agüero (superstition) says that if you stand a broom upside down behind the door without saying a word, who will leave the house?
hints: It's a trick for when you want your home to yourself again.
It works without traps or bug spray.
They are people who came over to the house.
questions.description: A broom doesn't just sweep away dust: according to grandmothers, it sweeps away other things too.
questions.fun_fact: Another broom agüero says that if someone sweeps over your feet, you'll never get married.

questions.question: In Colombia, which of these problems is NOT typical of the rainy season people call “invierno” (winter)?
hints: Think about what happens when a lot of water falls.
Three of these problems are caused by too much water.
The odd one out needs dry grass and heat.
questions.description: When the Colombian sky gets dramatic, grab your umbrella and your list of problems.
questions.fun_fact: In much of Colombia, April–May and October–November are usually the rainiest months.

questions.question: Look at the map: which department is home to the Combeima Canyon, which climbs toward a snow-capped peak?
hints: It's in central Colombia, between mountain ranges.
The canyon climbs up from the department's capital.
That capital is Ibagué, the “Musical City.”
questions.description: A canyon so green it's almost embarrassing to call it a canyon.
questions.fun_fact: The Combeima River, which carves the canyon, starts on the Nevado del Tolima and supplies water to Ibagué.

questions.question: Colombia's anthem starts with a glory that is “inmarcesible”. If a flower were inmarcesible, what would happen to it?
wrong_answers: It would glow in the dark
It would never lose its scent
hints: It has to do with the passing of time.
It's something that happens to flowers after a few days in a vase.
The word comes from Latin and is related to the Spanish verb “marchitar”.
questions.description: The strangest word in the anthem: everyone sings it, almost nobody dares to explain it.
questions.fun_fact: “Inmarcesible” comes from the Latin “marcescere”, which means to wither.

questions.question: In the Sumapaz páramo, signs warn about hypothermia. Finish this: “hypo” means “under” and “thermia” means…
hints: It comes from Greek.
It's in “thermometer” and “thermos”.
Its opposite is cold.
questions.description: A long word for something that happens to you very fast in the páramo.
questions.fun_fact: The Sumapaz páramo, south of Bogotá, is considered the largest páramo in the world.

questions.question: It's Colombia's largest coastal lagoon, between the Magdalena River and the Caribbean Sea, and home to Nueva Venecia, a village on stilts. What is it called?
hints: It's in the department of Magdalena.
Salamanca Island separates it from the sea.
It's named after Colombia's oldest city.
questions.description: A village with houses on the water: here, if you can't paddle, you can't get to the store.
questions.fun_fact: The Ciénaga Grande de Santa Marta is a Ramsar wetland and a UNESCO biosphere reserve.

questions.question: This animal is a Christmas dish in many Colombian homes. Which continent does it originally come from?
hints: Although it's eaten in Colombia today, it doesn't originally come from Colombia.
Wild turkeys still live in the forests of the continent it comes from.
It comes from the same continent as corn and potatoes.
questions.description: The star of Christmas dinner, who never asked to be invited.
questions.fun_fact: Ancient peoples of Mexico tamed the turkey about 2,000 years ago.

questions.question: Take a close look at this long, woody fruit: it's cañandonga, whose dark pulp is drunk with milk on the Caribbean coast. Which plant family does it belong to?
hints: Inside, it has many flat seeds in separate compartments.
It grows on a big tree with pink flowers, not on a palm.
It's the same family as beans, peas and tamarind.
questions.description: A fruit that looks like a club and smells like dirty socks, yet people still blend it with love.
questions.fun_fact: Cañandonga pulp smells so strong that many people hold their nose to drink it, but on the coast it's a traditional drink with milk.

questions.question: The palenqueras of Cartagena sing it, and sometimes it rhymes: it's the pregón. What is it for?
wrong_answers: To signal the stall has closed
hints: It's said before the customer shows up, not after.
It usually names fruits, sweets or fish.
It's like a commercial, but shouted in the street.
questions.description: Long before loudspeakers, the neighborhood already had its own sound system: a good pair of lungs.
questions.fun_fact: Street vendors' pregones have inspired many salsa and Caribbean songs.

questions.question: Before school, you have to iron your uniform. Why do people iron clothes?
hints: You do it on a long, narrow board.
You have to be careful not to burn yourself.
Afterward, the shirt is nice and smooth.
questions.description: On Sunday night, the school uniform goes to the spa.
questions.fun_fact: Before electric irons, people used heavy metal irons that were heated on the stove.

questions.question: It poisons rivers with mercury, leaves dredge holes in Chocó and the Amazon, and led to the Atrato River being declared a subject of rights. What is it?
hints: Park rangers and the security forces go after it.
It's looking for something at the bottom of rivers.
Its main goal is to get gold.
questions.description: A problem that leaves the rivers of the Pacific coast looking like they never want to get out of bed.
questions.fun_fact: In 2016, Colombia's Constitutional Court declared the Atrato River a subject of rights, something almost no river in the world had.

questions.question: In the Desfile de Silleteros, which category of silleta carries only bunches of flowers, with no figures or signs?
hints: It has no brands or ads.
It doesn't spell out messages or make pictures with flowers either.
It's put together the way the old silleteros of Santa Elena used to do it.
questions.description: A whole garden walking through Medellín on somebody's back.
questions.fun_fact: Before the Feria existed, the farmers of Santa Elena used the silleta to carry flowers down to sell in Medellín.

questions.question: I'm oval and sour, with red or orange skin. I'm blended into juice and ground with ají for empanadas. What am I?
hints: I grow in the Andes mountains, hanging from a small tree.
Inside I have little dark seeds and orange pulp.
My name puts together a salad vegetable and the place where I grow.
questions.description: The fruit that would rather end up in hot sauce than in dessert.
questions.fun_fact: Tomate de árbol is also called tamarillo, and it's a relative of the tomato and the potato.

questions.question: They talk to their plants, go grocery shopping in pajamas and sing at the top of their lungs on the bus. In Colombia, what do people say about them?
hints: It has nothing to do with money or with flirting.
It's said of someone who seems to have lost their mind.
The phrase is about something slipping out of place on a roof.
questions.description: For when someone's head is overdue for urgent maintenance.
questions.fun_fact: To say the same thing, Colombians also say someone «le falta un tornillo»: they're missing a screw.

questions.question: How often, and in which month, is the Carnaval de Riosucio in Caldas held?
hints: It isn't held every year.
During the festival, the matachines recite teasing verses.
It takes place in odd-numbered years, in the first days of the year.
questions.description: A party so good that even the devil asks permission to show up.
questions.fun_fact: The star of the Carnaval de Riosucio is the Devil, a cheerful, teasing character, not an evil one.

questions.question: The gaitas at the Ovejas gaita festival have a beeswax head and a duck-feather mouthpiece. What plant is their body made from?
hints: It's a plant of dry lands.
The craftsman scoops out its soft inner pulp.
It's a tall cactus that gets hollowed out to make the flute.
questions.description: In Ovejas (Spanish for “sheep”), Sucre, the sheep don't bleat: they blow.
questions.fun_fact: The Festival Nacional de Gaitas Francisco Llirene has been held in Ovejas, Sucre, since 1985.

questions.question: At a party where everyone dances, sings and has a great time, Colombians say: “¡Esto es una…!”
hints: It's something very cheerful.
It's said of a party nobody wants to leave.
It's also the title of a famous song by Gente de Zona and Marc Anthony.
questions.description: The exact opposite of an afternoon spent doing homework.
questions.fun_fact: “La Gozadera,” by Gente de Zona and Marc Anthony, names several Latin American countries, Colombia among them.

questions.question: In the Gran Cabalgata, thousands of riders parade on Paso Fino horses at a fair that starts in late December. In which city?
hints: The fair runs from December 25 to 30 and closes the year.
At the same fair, people dance in the Salsódromo.
It is the city of salsa.
questions.description: A parade where the ones walking with the most style have four legs.
questions.fun_fact: The Feria de Cali has been held since 1957, and every year it closes Colombia's calendar with horses, parades and salsa.

questions.question: You're at a street stand buying mango biche. Which of these do they NOT usually put on it?
hints: Mango biche is green and sour.
It's sold in little cups or bags on street corners and outside schools.
What doesn't go on it is something sweet you drink hot at breakfast.
questions.description: A fruit that isn't ripe yet but already has fans on every street corner.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “biche” means a fruit that isn't ripe yet.

questions.question: Sancocho trifásico has yuca, potato and plantain, and is cooked in a big pot on river outings. What does “trifásico” tell you?
wrong_answers: It is served in three bowls
hints: “Tri” means three.
The “three” is about what goes into the pot, not how it is cooked or served.
It has beef, pork and chicken in the same pot.
questions.description: A soup with so much energy, its name sounds like it came off a fuse box.
questions.fun_fact: “Trifásico” comes from electricity: three-phase power has three phases, just as the sancocho has three meats.

questions.question: You buy maíz peto at the market. Which of these dishes is NOT made with corn?
hints: The odd one out is typical of the Caribbean coast, especially Córdoba and Sucre.
It's eaten hot and served with white rice.
It's thickened with ñame, a root vegetable.
questions.description: A market where corn is the boss, but someone sneaked onto the list.
questions.fun_fact: In Antioquia, mazamorra made with maíz peto is drunk with milk and a piece of panela or bocadillo.

questions.question: This village in the Sierra Nevada belongs to Valledupar and is the main town of the Kankuamo people. What is it called?
hints: It sits on the slopes of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, on the Cesar side.
The chicote, a traditional dance, is danced there.
Its name starts with A.
questions.description: A town so high up in the Sierra that vallenato arrives there a little out of breath.
questions.fun_fact: Several vallenato songwriters come from Atánquez, where Indigenous music and the accordion met.

questions.question: You're making a poster for school: “scissors” is to cutting as “colbón” is to…
hints: Colbón comes in a bottle and it's white.
If it gets on your fingers, it dries and peels off like skin.
It keeps the paper shapes from falling off the poster board.
questions.description: The school poster at 10 p.m.: the real test for parents.
questions.fun_fact: “Colbón” started out as a brand name and ended up as every Colombian's word for white glue.

questions.question: Rapunzel let me grow longer and longer, Elsa wears me in a braid, and in Colombia anyone who has me is called «mono». What am I?
hints: Rapunzel and Elsa have the same hair color.
My color looks like the sun or gold.
I'm light hair, almost yellow.
questions.description: In Colombia, this nickname has nothing to do with climbing trees or eating bananas.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, babies with very light hair are lovingly called «monitos».

questions.question: Its followers are called “godos,” its color is blue, and Mariano Ospina Rodríguez and José Eusebio Caro founded it in 1849. Which party is it?
hints: It's one of Colombia's two traditional parties.
Its historic rival is the red party.
Its name comes from wanting to conserve traditions.
questions.description: In Colombia, politics was all about colors, and not because of fashion.
questions.fun_fact: Conservatives and Liberals took turns in power in Colombia for more than a century.

questions.question: In Colombia, if someone says their motorcycle cost “dos barras,” how much money did they pay?
hints: It's much more than a few lucas.
A “barra” is the same amount as a “palo.”
Each barra has six zeros.
questions.description: A word that sounds like a candy bar, but it's worth way more.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombian slang, “un palo” and “una barra” mean the same thing: one million pesos.

questions.question: You see a price with the “$” sign in a shop window. In which of these countries is that sign NOT used for its currency?
hints: Three of these countries have a currency called the peso.
The country you're looking for has a currency named after the Sun.
There, prices are written with “S/”.
questions.description: An S with a line through it that shows up in every shop window in the neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: The $ sign was used for the peso before it was used for the US dollar.

questions.question: Ego is a Colombian shampoo and hair gel brand from the company behind Savital and Bon Ice. Who was it made for?
hints: Its gel is famous for hairstyles with a really strong hold.
Its name is about self-confidence.
On the bottle, “Ego” is followed by two English words saying who it's for.
questions.description: A shampoo with so much self-esteem that it named itself after it.
questions.fun_fact: Quala, the company behind Ego, also makes Doña Gallina bouillon cubes.

questions.question: It was born on Colombia’s Caribbean coast, is sung mostly by older women called cantadoras, and has its national festival in Necoclí. What accompanies the singing in bullerengue?
hints: It has no wind instruments at all.
It’s sung in a circle: the cantadora calls out a verse and the chorus answers.
It’s all percussion: beaten drumheads and clapping hands.
questions.description: A party where the grandmas sing louder than any speaker.
questions.fun_fact: Petrona Martínez, the great queen of bullerengue, was nominated for the Latin Grammy several times.

questions.question: At the Carnaval de Barranquilla, people throw things at each other for fun. Which of these do they NOT throw?
hints: Three of them don’t leave your clothes sticky.
The odd one out goes on your toast.
It’s sweet and made from fruit.
questions.description: A battle where everyone loses and everyone leaves happy.
questions.fun_fact: At the carnival, lots of people wear goggles to protect their eyes from foam and cornstarch.

questions.question: “I’m in Neiva, on the banks of the Magdalena River, and Atlético Huila plays its home games on my grass.” What’s my name?
hints: All four are names of Colombian stadiums that honor a person.
My name honors a politician from Huila itself.
My name has a double surname: Plazas…
questions.description: A field where the heat of the San Pedro festival reaches all the way into the locker rooms.
questions.fun_fact: Atlético Huila’s women’s team won the Copa Libertadores Femenina in 2018, the first continental title for a Colombian women’s club.

questions.question: The club nicknamed “la Naranja Mecánica” wears orange, trained James Rodríguez in its youth system and comes from a town next to Medellín. Which one?
hints: It’s in the Aburrá Valley, south of Medellín.
Its stadium is called the Polideportivo Sur.
The club has the same name as the town, followed by “Fútbol Club”.
questions.description: A club so orange it looks like orange juice wearing cleats.
questions.fun_fact: The nickname, Spanish for “the Clockwork Orange”, comes from the Netherlands team of the 1970s, famous for its orange shirts and its “Total Football”.

questions.question: On TV you see the soccer score “Junior 0–1 Nacional”. By custom, the team listed first is…
hints: It has nothing to do with the goals.
It has to do with the stadium where the game is played.
Its fans usually fill most of the stadium.
questions.description: In math, the order doesn’t change the answer; on a scoreboard, it says quite a lot.
questions.fun_fact: Playing at home is a real advantage: in almost every league in the world, teams win more games in their own stadium.

questions.question: In the Colombian countryside, people say that where a little flame rises from the ground at night, there's an “entierro”. What is that entierro?
hints: They say spirits guard it and don't let just anyone come near.
Whoever found it would get rich overnight.
They say it's full of gold coins from colonial times.
questions.description: The stories grandparents tell by the wood stove when the power goes out in the countryside.
questions.fun_fact: “Guaca”, another word for buried treasure, gives us “guaquero”: someone who hunts for buried treasure.

questions.question: I was born in Medellín, got famous with videos of my life on YouTube and Instagram, and I'm the mom of Máximo, son of singer Pipe Bueno. Who am I?
hints: She's one of the most-followed influencers in Colombia.
She's paisa, not costeña or rola.
Her stage name ends with a single letter.
questions.description: A paisa with more followers than many countries have people.
questions.fun_fact: Besides creating content, Luisa Fernanda W has also launched a career as a singer.

questions.question: Boyacomán gets laughs playing a farmer from Boyacá, and like a true boyacense he treats everyone with warmth. What word does he use instead of “usted”?
hints: You also hear it a lot in Bogotá and Cundinamarca.
It comes from an old, respectful way of speaking.
It's a contraction of “su merced”.
questions.description: A comedian who brings the chill of the high plains and a hug in every word.
questions.fun_fact: “Sumercé” comes from “su merced” (“your grace”), a respectful form of old Spanish that is still alive and well in Boyacá and Cundinamarca.

questions.question: A Colombian agüero (superstition) for a good day, done as you get out of bed: hence “empezar con buen pie” (start with a good foot). Which foot goes first?
hints: It's just one foot.
According to the superstition, the other foot brings bad luck.
The opposite of left.
questions.description: A very important decision you make before your eyes are even fully open.
questions.fun_fact: Many Colombians also step into a new house or into the New Year with their right foot, so luck comes along with them.

questions.question: In this sport, which Colombian woman won Olympic bronze at London 2012 and silver at Rio 2016?
hints: She is from Valle del Cauca.
She was judo world champion several times.
She was born in Jamundí and her last name starts with A.
questions.description: A sport where the white uniform is definitely not pajamas.
questions.fun_fact: Yuri Alvear was judo world champion three times: in 2009, 2013 and 2014.

questions.question: You're at the Édgar Rentería stadium in Barranquilla watching baseball. How many players does the fielding team have on the field?
hints: More than a basketball team, fewer than a soccer team.
That includes the pitcher and the catcher.
The same as the number of innings in a regular game.
questions.description: On Colombia's Caribbean coast, people argue about this sport more passionately than about the price of fish.

review.feedback: Source: the fun fact says that in Colombia "llanta" means both the tire and the whole wheel. That can't be confirmed. In Colombian usage "llanta" mainly means the tire, "rin" is the rim and "rueda" is the wheel. The fact check rates it wrong. The source's fun fact needs to be replaced with a fact that can be checked, for example about "cicla" being everyday Colombian slang or about the Sunday ciclovía. Then this translation should be redone from the new source. Fact check: wrong. The math is right (4×2 + 2×3 = 14) and the wrong answers are wrong. The fun fact is not accurate. In Colombia "llanta" mainly means the rubber tire, and "rin" is the metal rim. It is not the standard word for the whole wheel (that is "rueda"). Some sources say "llanta" can mean the rim on a bicycle, and shops sometimes use it loosely for the whole assembly.
