hints: Its dark, slightly greenish color is a clue.
It's a metal, not a stone.
It's the same material as third-place medals.
questions.description: Almost two centuries standing in the square, and still not a single day off.
questions.fun_fact: It was made by the Italian sculptor Pietro Tenerani.

questions.question: The Botero Museum in Bogotá's La Candelaria opened in 2000 from the artist's donation and is free. Besides his own works, what does it hold?
questions.answer: Works by Picasso, Dalí and other masters
hints: Botero was also a great collector.
Many of those pieces come from Europe.
There are paintings by very famous 20th-century painters.
questions.description: A museum where nobody is on a diet, not even the fruit.
questions.fun_fact: Botero donated more than 200 works, some his own and some by other artists.

questions.question: Your tinto comes from Castillo, Cenicafé's coffee bred to resist leaf rust. It's a cross of Caturra with which other coffee?
hints: It appeared on its own on a plantation in the 20th century and is behind many rust-resistant coffees around the world.
It came from a natural cross between arabica and robusta coffee.
Its island is split between Indonesia and a country that became independent in 2002.
questions.description: A coffee in armor, raised in a lab to fight off fungi.
questions.fun_fact: The Castillo variety, released by Cenicafé in 2005, is named after Colombian researcher Jaime Castillo Zapata.

questions.question: I'm flat as far as the eye can see, my cowboys sing as they herd cattle, and harp, cuatro and maracas play at my parties. Which region am I?
hints: People dance joropo at my parties.
My lands are also called the Llanos Orientales (Eastern Plains).
My name comes from a big river I share with Venezuela.
questions.description: The horizon here is so flat you can see Saturday's rainstorm coming on Tuesday.
questions.fun_fact: In the Llanos, the canto de vaquería is a tune llaneros sing to calm the cattle while they herd them.

questions.question: Restaurants in Colombia ask if you want to add an extra 10% for the waiters. What is that payment called?
hints: It isn't a tax.
Paying it is optional.
It goes to the person who served you, as a thank-you.
questions.description: That little number at the bottom of the bill that makes everyone at the table look at each other.
questions.fun_fact: Colombian law says the propina is optional, and the restaurant must ask you before adding it to the bill.

questions.question: Commentators say a cyclist “came in with the grupeta.” What is the grupeta?
questions.answer: The group of stragglers at the back
wrong_answers: The breakaway group out in front
The convoy of team support cars
hints: The word comes from the Italian “gruppetto.”
It's usually where the riders who aren't climbers end up.
If they reach the finish too late, they're out of the race.
questions.description: A word that sounds like a weekend bike ride with your friends.
questions.fun_fact: In the grupeta, riders from different teams work together so they don't get eliminated for finishing outside the time limit.

questions.question: Look at the photo: it's limoncillo, used for the herbal tea that smells like lemon. What kind of plant is it really?
questions.answer: A grass in the wheat family
wrong_answers: A shrub in the lemon tree family
A plant in the mint family
A vine in the vanilla family
hints: It has nothing to do with citrus fruits.
Its long, thin leaves all grow straight from the ground, with no trunk or branches.
It's in the same family as sugarcane.
questions.description: Grandma swears this cures everything, from a cold to a bad mood.
questions.fun_fact: Limoncillo's lemon smell comes from citral, the same scented substance found in lemon peel.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: El Totumo, near Cartagena, is famous for being a volcano of…
hints: Tourists climb inside and come out without getting burned.
Afterward, you have to wash off in the lagoon next door.
You come out brown and sticky from head to toe.
questions.description: A tiny volcano with a giant reputation among tourists.
questions.fun_fact: People say nobody sinks in El Totumo's crater: the mud is so thick that you float.

questions.question: British rider Bethany Shriever beat Mariana Pajón in the Tokyo Olympic final. In what year was that final?
hints: It was a very unusual edition of the Olympics.
With that silver, Pajón completed three Olympic medals in a row.
It was one year after the year in the name of those Games.
questions.description: Jumps, tight turns and a paisa whose trophy cabinet is already full of medals.
questions.fun_fact: Bethany Shriever had to raise money online to pay for part of her Olympic training.

questions.question: It comes from Quechua, it's used in Nariño and in Ecuador, and it names the little hollow in the belly where a baby's cord was. What's the word?
hints: It's a very short word.
Everyone has had one since the day they were born.
Elsewhere in Colombia it's called the “ombligo”.
questions.description: A word every one of us carries right in the middle of the tummy.
questions.fun_fact: In Nariño people also say “guagua” for a baby and “chuspa” for a bag, both from Quechua, and “taita” for dad, a word used across the Andes.

questions.question: Luis Soriano carries books to the rural villages of Magdalena on his donkeys, Alfa and Beto. Where do their names come from?
hints: It has to do with learning to read.
Think of the first thing you learn at school so you can read.
It's the list of all the letters, from A to Z.
questions.description: The most stubborn library in the world, and not because of the books.
questions.fun_fact: The Biblioburro of La Gloria, Magdalena, became so famous that it inspired documentaries and children's books in other countries.

questions.question: Look at this close-up: it's black, in Colombia it's stuffed with rice, and no picada is complete without it. What is it?
hints: It's a pork sausage.
Its dark color comes from blood.
In some regions it's also called rellena.
questions.description: A sausage that always has a line at the fritanga stand.
questions.fun_fact: In parts of Colombia, morcilla is called “rellena”, and in Bogotá people often eat it with papa criolla.

questions.question: You eat a Gansito at recess. Who is the Ramo brand named after?
hints: He founded the company in Bogotá.
The name joins the start of his first name and the start of his last name.
RA from his first name and MO from his last name.
questions.description: A goose that has traveled in lunchboxes for decades and never once flown.
questions.fun_fact: Rafael Molano started out selling homemade cakes before creating one of Colombia's best-loved brands.

questions.question: Jesús María Ocampo, who founded Armenia in 1889, was known to everyone as “el…”. How does his nickname end?
hints: The nickname comes from a reputation he had in the wilderness, before he founded the city.
He earned it for his bravery in a very risky trade in the region's forests.
Country people back then called the jaguar “tigre.”
questions.description: Founding a city is easy; earning a nickname like that in Quindío is the hard part.
questions.fun_fact: Armenia is called “la Ciudad Milagro” (the Miracle City) because it grew so fast after it was founded.

questions.question: If you laugh at Andrés López's “La pelota de letras,” whose childhood are you remembering?
questions.answer: People who grew up in the '70s and '80s
wrong_answers: People who grew up in the '50s and '60s
People who grew up in the '90s and 2000s
People who grew up in the '30s and '40s
hints: Andrés López looks back at the toys, TV shows and scoldings from Mom of his own childhood.
TV had only a few channels, and kids played games out in the street.
There was already color TV and the first video game consoles were arriving, but no internet.
questions.description: A comedy show that makes parents feel old in under two hours.
questions.fun_fact: “La pelota de letras” became one of the most-watched comedy shows in Colombia and was released on DVD.

questions.question: In the Colombian Amazon it's toasted on big budares (griddles), it's grainy and yellowish, and it goes into fish broth. What is fariña?
hints: Its name comes from Portuguese, because Brazil is right next door.
It's sold by the sack at the Leticia market and eaten daily there, like rice.
It comes from a root that is poisonous if it isn't processed.
questions.description: Golden jungle sand that, luckily, you can actually eat.
questions.fun_fact: Yuca brava has a toxic juice that Amazon peoples learned to squeeze out before toasting it.

questions.question: Listen: which instrument is this?
hints: You play it by opening and closing one part, as if it were breathing.
It has buttons or keys on both sides.
It's the main instrument of vallenato.
questions.description: An instrument that never misses a party and always shows up ready to dance.
questions.fun_fact: The accordion came to Colombia from Europe by ship and ended up as the king of vallenato.

questions.question: Look at this pelican from the beaches of Santa Marta. What does it use the pouch under its beak for?
wrong_answers: To store food for several days
hints: It dives headfirst into the water
It works like a net
It lets the water drain out and swallows its catch
questions.description: A bird with more pockets than a pair of cargo pants.
questions.fun_fact: A pelican's pouch can hold about 10 liters (2.5 gallons) of water.

questions.question: Look at this toad. How many legs does it have?
hints: It has legs in the front and in the back
The back ones are longer for jumping
It has the same number as a dog
questions.description: In Colombia a «sapo» is someone who tells on everybody; this one only tells you how far it jumped.
questions.fun_fact: Most toads have 4 toes on their front feet and 5 on their back feet.

questions.question: Conchita appears with Juan Valdez in the ads and the famous logo. What is her job?
hints: She's a pack animal.
She walks the coffee mountains with something on her back.
She brings the harvest down from the farm.
questions.description: The most patient coworker in all of Colombian advertising.
questions.fun_fact: Conchita is a mule, the offspring of a donkey and a horse, an animal widely used to climb Colombia's steep coffee farms.

questions.question: Lin-Manuel Miranda wrote it, Sebastián Yatra sings it, and it was nominated for the Oscar for Best Original Song. Which film is “Dos Oruguitas” from?
hints: It's a Disney film.
In the film, the song goes with the memory of how a grandmother lost her husband and found a new home.
Mirabel and the Madrigal family's house are in it.
questions.description: Two little bugs that made it all the way to the world's most famous red carpet.
questions.fun_fact: Sebastián Yatra sang “Dos Oruguitas” live at the 2022 Oscars ceremony.

questions.question: Sabajón, a Christmas drink of egg, milk and liquor, has relatives in other countries. Which of these drinks is NOT one of them?
hints: Look for the drink with no egg and no milk.
It's drunk hot on cold nights in the Andes.
It's made with aguapanela, cinnamon and aguardiente.
questions.description: A very creamy family Christmas party, with one cousin who looks like nobody else.
questions.fun_fact: The name “sabajón” comes from zabaione, an Italian cream made of egg yolks, sugar and wine.

questions.question: In many Colombian towns, people drink chicha or water from a totuma. What is a totuma made from?
questions.answer: A tree's dried fruit, cut in half
wrong_answers: A cut piece of guadua bamboo
hints: No potter makes it.
It grows hanging from branches, green and round.
The tree is called the totumo.
questions.description: Grandma's favorite cup for chicha, and it tastes better than any glass.
questions.fun_fact: The same totumo fruit is used to make the maracas heard in music from Colombia's Caribbean coast.

questions.question: I'm a Colombian actress. In “Birds of Passage” by Ciro Guerra and Cristina Gallego, I played Úrsula, the Wayuu matriarch who defends her clan. Who am I?
hints: The film is set in La Guajira during the bonanza marimbera.
My character guards her Wayuu family's traditions and dreams.
My first name is a diminutive of Carmen.
questions.description: A grandmother nobody in the clan dares to argue with.
questions.fun_fact: “Birds of Passage” was Colombia's submission for the Oscar for best foreign language film.

questions.question: Colombia's coat of arms shows an open pomegranate with its red seeds visible. What does it recall?
questions.answer: The country's old name, New Granada
wrong_answers: The harvests of the Valle del Cauca
hints: It has nothing to do with food.
It has to do with what the land was called centuries ago.
In colonial times, this land was the New Kingdom of…
questions.description: A fruit with more seeds than there are speeches in a session of Congress.
questions.fun_fact: The New Kingdom of Granada was named after the Spanish city of Granada, whose symbol is also this fruit.

questions.question: You're in Bogotá's Plaza de Bolívar. Which of these places is NOT on the square?
hints: The square is the city's historic heart, where Bogotá was founded.
The place that isn't there lies several kilometers north of La Candelaria.
Millonarios and Santa Fe play there.
questions.description: A square where the pigeons have more power than many politicians.
questions.fun_fact: The square's Bolívar statue, made by the Italian Pietro Tenerani, was Bogotá's first public statue.

questions.question: I hosted the 1972 Olympic Games, where Colombia won its first medals: a silver in shooting and two bronzes in boxing. Who am I?
hints: Those Games had the first official Olympic mascot, a little dachshund.
I am a European city.
I am the capital of Bavaria, in Germany.
questions.description: The place where Colombia finally got to fill its Olympic trophy cabinet.
questions.fun_fact: The Munich silver was won by Helmut Bellingrodt from Barranquilla, in running target shooting.

questions.question: In which decade was Miguel “Happy” Lora, from Montería, the WBC bantamweight world champion?
hints: It was after the days of Kid Pambelé.
He won the title in the middle of the decade and defended it several times.
He took the belt from Daniel Zaragoza in 1985.
questions.description: The boxer from Córdoba who proved you can punch hard and still be called “Happy.”
questions.fun_fact: Happy Lora held the WBC bantamweight title from 1985 until he lost it in 1988, defending it several times along the way.

questions.question: I have pages of animals, planets and landscapes, filled with stickers that come inside a chocolate bar. Kids trade their duplicates at school. What am I?
hints: I’m Colombian, and several generations have filled me.
My stickers aren’t sold in packets: they come with a treat.
The chocolate bar that feeds me has a three-letter name, like a fast airplane.
questions.description: Collecting with discipline and eating chocolate guilt-free: the perfect plan.
questions.fun_fact: Jet stickers have fun facts on the back, so you learn while you collect.

questions.question: Rafael Pombo was a member of the Colombian Academy of Language, the oldest such academy in the Americas. In what year was it founded?
hints: Colombia had already been independent for several decades.
Its founders included Miguel Antonio Caro and Rufino José Cuervo.
It was just one year after Charles Dickens died in 1870.
questions.description: The official guards making sure nobody ever says “haiga” or “nadien.”
questions.fun_fact: Rufino José Cuervo, one of its founders, started a dictionary so huge that it was finished almost a century after his death.

questions.question: You're listening to Shakira's session with Bizarrap. In the lyrics, “Ferrari” is to “Twingo” as “Rolex” is to…
hints: Shakira compares very expensive things with much cheaper ones.
In the song, the cheap watch stands for the new partner, who is worth far less than she is.
It's a brand famous for its calculators and the digital watch lots of students wear.
questions.description: A recording session that ended up costing more than a divorce.
questions.fun_fact: Shakira's BZRP Music Session #53 broke several YouTube records in its first 24 hours.

questions.question: Whose 2018 album “Vibras” includes hits like “Ambiente” and “Machika”?
hints: He's a man, a reggaeton artist from Medellín.
He's called “the Prince of Reggaeton” and loves dyeing his hair.
“Mi gente” is on that same album.
questions.description: An album that could get even grandma dancing reggaeton, with her doctor's permission.
questions.fun_fact: “Vibras” won the Latin Grammy for Best Urban Music Album in 2018.

questions.question: “We Don't Talk About Bruno” is a song from a Disney movie. In which country is that movie set?
hints: It's a country of coffee, mountains and yellow butterflies.
The family lives in a magical house among coffee-growing mountains.
Its capital is Bogotá.
questions.description: A song about someone nobody talks about… that nobody can stop singing.
questions.fun_fact: “We Don't Talk About Bruno” reached number one on the US charts, something no Disney song had done since the 1990s.

questions.question: Carranga singers perform in a ruana and a light, hand-woven hat that keeps the sun off. What is that hat made of?
hints: It's a material that comes from plants.
It's dry stalks, like the ones spread on the floor of a barn.
It's yellow, and it's also used to stuff scarecrows.
questions.description: The only roof a farmer ever wears on his head.
questions.fun_fact: Jorge Velosa, the father of carranga, almost always goes on stage in a ruana and hat, dressed like a farmer from Boyacá.

review.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. I couldn't confirm the hat is straw. Sources confirm the ruana and hat are the carranga look and that Jorge Velosa wears both. Some sources mention a straw campesino hat (e.g. the jipa). Boyacá campesino hats are also often felt (wool). Velosa's own hat is usually a dark felt one, which would make 'Wool' arguably correct. No source I found says what the carranga hat is made of. The question's 'light, hand-woven' wording favours straw. The fun fact is broadly true.

questions.question: Los Tolimenses became famous for funny country songs. How many members did the group have?
hints: Their name already tells you which region of Colombia they came from.
Each one had a country-style nickname.
They called themselves “Emeterio y Felipe.”
questions.description: Jokes, folk verses and a guitar: the recipe for making the whole village laugh.
questions.fun_fact: Besides singing, Los Tolimenses told jokes and made radio shows starring country characters.

questions.question: It's sold from carts on the street and comes in lots of colors. What is a Bon Ice?
questions.answer: A flavored ice in a little tube
wrong_answers: A shaved ice with syrup in a little cup
A frozen fruit pop on a little stick
An ice cream sandwich in a little wrapper
hints: It's sweet, and mostly kids eat it.
It comes in blackberry, lime and mango, and you find it in parks and outside schools.
You bite off one end and squeeze it up as you eat.
questions.description: A street-cart classic that every Colombian kid has asked for at least once.
questions.fun_fact: To eat one, you bite or cut off the tip of the tube and suck it before it melts.

questions.question: You're having Corona hot chocolate for breakfast. How long ago was its maker, the Compañía Nacional de Chocolates, founded in Medellín?
hints: Your grandparents were already drinking this company's chocolate as kids.
It was founded early in the 20th century.
It was founded in 1920.
questions.description: A company that has been sneaking into your breakfast for decades without asking.
questions.fun_fact: The Compañía Nacional de Chocolates is now part of Grupo Nutresa, one of Colombia's largest food companies.

questions.question: Tourists come to Minca, in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, to look for the animal group in which Colombia has more species than any other country. Which group is it?
hints: Sometimes all you have to do to see them is look up.
Visitors get up very early to see and hear them.
Hummingbirds and toucans belong to this group.
questions.description: In this Sierra village, your tinto comes with a jungle view and a blanket of fog.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia has more than 1,900 recorded bird species, more than any other country in the world.

questions.question: Hip hop has four elements: rap, DJing, breakdancing and one more that turned Medellín's Comuna 13 into an open-air museum. Which one?
hints: The fourth element isn't something you hear: you look at it.
Tourists walk around Comuna 13 taking photos of its walls.
It's made with cans of paint on walls.
questions.description: Some bring the beat, some bring the rhymes, some bring the moves; somebody had to handle the decorating.
questions.fun_fact: Comuna 13 has outdoor escalators that help residents climb the neighborhood's steep hills.

questions.question: In Colombia, a paradero usually has a little roof, a bench and a sign with route numbers. What is it for?
hints: People stand there for a while.
When you see your route coming, you stick out your hand.
Passengers get on and off there.
questions.description: A place where patience is measured in minutes and hope at every corner.
questions.fun_fact: In systems like TransMilenio, the paradero is called an “estación”, and you can only get in by paying with a card.

questions.question: In a vallenato group, one item is called a “trinche.” What is it?
hints: It's made of metal and has several thin prongs.
In many Colombian homes, “trinche” is another word for a fork.
The musician who plays the grooved cane instrument uses it.
questions.description: A word that means one thing in the kitchen and something very different on the vallenato stage.
questions.fun_fact: A traditional guacharaca is made of cane or palm, with grooves carved into it so it can be scraped.

questions.question: San Andrés airport is named Gustavo Rojas Pinilla, after a former president. Which of these airports is NOT named after a president?
hints: The one you want was a military hero of independence.
He is remembered for shouting “¡Armas a discreción, paso de vencedores!”
It is the airport that serves Medellín.
questions.description: Landing in Colombia is basically a history class with your seatbelt on.
questions.fun_fact: Gustavo Rojas Pinilla ruled from 1953 to 1957, and television arrived in Colombia under his government, in 1954.

questions.question: You're having a corrientazo for lunch, and next to the rice comes a shredded cabbage salad. What orange vegetable is usually mixed in with the cabbage?
hints: It's eaten raw, grated into thin strips.
People say it's good for your eyesight.
It's the favorite food of cartoon rabbits.
questions.description: The salad everyone leaves for last and then fights over.
questions.fun_fact: The “corrientazo” is the set lunch of the day at Colombia's everyday restaurants, with soup, a main plate and juice.

questions.question: Finish the line from Rafael Pombo's poem: the poor little old woman left only “gold coins, jewels, lands, houses, … cats and a turpial.” How many?
hints: The poem exaggerates everything the old woman owned.
She had more cats than fingers on one hand.
It's the number that looks like two wheels stacked on top of each other.
questions.description: Colombia's “poorest” lady, with houses, jewels and pets to spare.
questions.fun_fact: The joke of the poem is that the old woman is called “poor,” but she had everything.

questions.question: This is the Astronomical Observatory of Bogotá, one of the first in the Americas. Which scholar was its first director?
hints: He was a criollo, born in New Granada.
He worked on the Royal Botanical Expedition.
He was called “el Sabio” (the Wise One), and a department bears his surname.
questions.description: A building for stargazing back when Bogotá didn't even have light bulbs.
questions.fun_fact: The Bogotá observatory was finished in 1803 and is said to be the first of its kind in the Americas.

questions.question: Today's Colombian bills have raised marks you can feel with your finger. Who are they mainly meant for?
questions.answer: People who are blind or have low vision
hints: They help some people handle their money on their own.
You use touch instead of your eyes.
They work a bit like braille.
questions.description: Paper with national heroes, flowers and animals that everyone wants in their pocket.
questions.fun_fact: On today's Colombian bills, each value has a different size: the more a bill is worth, the longer it is.

questions.question: It’s a hot drink from Nariño made with fruit juice like lulo, blackberry or passion fruit, and its name says how it’s made. What is it?
hints: People drink a lot of it on the cold nights of the Carnaval de Negros y Blancos.
It’s sold steaming on the street, from big pots.
Its name comes from what happens to water at 100 °C (212 °F).
questions.description: In chilly Pasto, no jacket will do the job: you need a cup.
questions.fun_fact: In Pasto, adults order it “con” (with) or “sin” (without), meaning with or without a splash of aguardiente.

questions.question: Medellín’s Desfile de Mitos y Leyendas brings out characters from Colombian folklore. Which of these is NOT a Colombian myth?
hints: Three of them haunt Colombia’s hills and rivers.
The odd one out comes from Guaraní tradition.
It’s famous in Paraguay and northern Argentina.
questions.description: A parade where the spooks come out in broad daylight and people clap.
questions.fun_fact: The Desfile de Mitos y Leyendas is part of the Feria de las Flores and has giant floats with spooks from paisa folklore.

questions.question: I'm made of fique or plastic fiber. Coteros carry me on their shoulders at the market, filled with about 50 kg (110 lb) of potatoes. What am I called in Colombia?
hints: At the plaza de mercado, people buy wholesale this way.
That's why someone who never moves is said to look like one.
It's a big, tightly stuffed sack.
questions.description: It weighs more than your school backpack on a Monday morning.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, when someone plays badly in a match, people say they were “como un bulto”: all weight and no movement.

questions.question: The palenqueras come from San Basilio de Palenque. In colonial times, what was a “palenque”?
questions.answer: A village behind a stake fence where people who escaped slavery lived
wrong_answers: An open-air market where Caribbean fruits were sold
A stone fort where the Spanish kept watch over the port
A large hacienda where sugarcane was grown
hints: They were hidden in the wild, far from the cities.
The people who lived there were called cimarrones.
The word comes from the posts, or stakes, that surrounded the place.
questions.description: Long before it rang out on Cartagena's beaches next to the cocadas, this word meant something else.
questions.fun_fact: San Basilio de Palenque, whose history is tied to the rebel leader Benkos Biohó, was recognized by UNESCO as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: In the Eje Cafetero, the season comes when pickers fill their baskets with ripe red coffee cherries. What is it called?
hints: It happens when the fruit is finally ready.
It comes after planting and waiting.
It's when you gather what was planted.
questions.description: In the Eje Cafetero, even the mountains wake up smelling of tinto.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia has two coffee harvests a year: the main one and a smaller one called the “traviesa” or “mitaca.”

questions.question: It's December 31, minutes before midnight, and in many Colombian homes people sweep from inside toward the door. Why?
questions.answer: To get rid of the year's bad luck
wrong_answers: To make it rain in January
hints: It's one of the New Year's agüeros, like the grapes or the yellow underwear.
It's about what you don't want to carry into the new year.
The bad stuff from the old year goes out the door with the dust.
questions.description: When the year runs out, even a broom gets superpowers.
questions.fun_fact: Another Colombian New Year's agüero is carrying lentils in your pocket or wallet so you never run short of money.

questions.question: It's always on the preschool supply list: it comes in colored sticks, you knead it with your hands and make little figures with it. What is it?
hints: It's a cheap supply that kids love to use in art class.
It doesn't dry out, so you can use it again and again.
You roll it into little snakes and balls.
questions.description: What starts on the supply list ends up on the sofa, in your hair and even on the dog.
questions.fun_fact: Plasticine was invented in England in 1897, and it doesn't dry out even if you leave it out.

questions.question: Which popular leader from Pasto kept fighting for the King of Spain until 1824, when independence had already been won?
hints: He came from a humble background and rose to colonel in the king's army.
In 1824 he attacked the town of Barbacoas, on the Pacific coast.
His surname begins with the Spanish word for water.
questions.description: While half the continent shouted “Long live independence!”, someone in the south was shouting something else.
questions.fun_fact: Today many people in Pasto remember him as a local hero, and he even has a monument in the city.

questions.question: Colombia’s Ministry of Culture coordinates the law that protects the country’s native languages. In which decade was that ministry created?
hints: Before it existed, culture was handled by a smaller institute called Colcultura.
It was created by the General Law of Culture.
It came a few years after the 1991 Constitution.
questions.description: Even culture needs someone to do its paperwork.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia’s Ministry of Culture was born with Law 397 of 1997.

questions.question: In Colombia you can call a friend «socio». Which of these words is NOT used in Colombia to mean the same?
hints: You hear three of these words on any street corner in Colombia.
The odd one out is heard a lot in another country’s films and telenovelas.
It’s the typical way to say “friend” in Mexico.
questions.description: In Colombia there are more words for “friend” than actual friends.
questions.fun_fact: «Cuate» comes from the Nahuatl «cóatl», meaning “snake” and also “twin”, which is why in Mexico «cuate» can also mean a twin.

questions.question: I'm a stretch of rapids and rocks on the Orinoco River in Vichada, next to El Tuparro park. Alexander von Humboldt called me “the eighth wonder of the world.” What am I?
hints: I'm on the border between Colombia and Venezuela.
My name comes from an Indigenous people who lived in that part of the Orinoco.
My name starts with “Mai…”.
questions.description: A stretch of river so wild that even a German scientist was left speechless.
questions.fun_fact: Humboldt passed through these rapids in 1800, during his famous journey along the Orinoco.

questions.question: About how many protected areas are in Colombia's National Natural Parks System?
hints: There are more than you can count on one hand.
It includes parks, flora and fauna sanctuaries, and reserves.
More than 50 but fewer than 100.
questions.description: A sticker album that collects jungles, páramos and reefs instead of soccer players.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's first national park was Cueva de los Guácharos, in Huila, created in 1960.

questions.question: I have four wheels and an engine, I ride close to the ground, and I have no roof or doors. Juan Pablo Montoya started racing me as a kid in Bogotá. What am I?
hints: There are tracks for me in several Colombian cities, even in some shopping malls.
Many Formula 1 drivers start out with me as kids.
Mario and Luigi race me too in a very famous video game.
questions.description: A real car that shrank in the wash but still goes super fast.
questions.fun_fact: Montoya started karting at age 6 and went on to win Formula 1 races in Monaco and Monza.

questions.question: Johnny Cay is a small cay a few minutes by boat from San Andrés, full of palm trees and white sand. What is it made of?
hints: It formed little by little in the sea.
Tiny living things built it.
Its sand comes from the reefs around it.
questions.description: An island so tiny you can walk around it before your raspado melts.
questions.fun_fact: The San Andrés islands are part of the Seaflower Biosphere Reserve, declared by UNESCO in 2000.

questions.question: I'm round and flat, people made me from corn before the Spanish arrived, and you eat me for breakfast with butter and cheese. What am I?
hints: I'm cooked on a grill or on a clay griddle called a tiesto.
There are chócolo, egg and cheese versions of me.
My name starts with “a”.
questions.description: A recipe older than your grandparents' grandparents' grandparents.
questions.fun_fact: Indigenous peoples were already grinding corn on stones to make arepas centuries before Spanish rule.

questions.question: Look at this flag: which country is it from?
hints: It's a South American country with coasts on two oceans.
Its flag has the same colors as a neighbor's, but with no coat of arms in the middle.
It's the country of Encanto, coffee and Shakira.
questions.description: A question so easy that even the family parrot knows the answer.
questions.fun_fact: The yellow stripe takes up half of the Colombian flag: it's twice as wide as the blue and the red ones.

questions.question: In which decade was Leonisa, the underwear and swimwear brand from Medellín, founded?
hints: It's older than most of the parents who buy it.
It was born shortly after television arrived in Colombia.
It was born in the middle of the 20th century.
questions.description: Paisa fashion that has seen a whole lot of beach seasons come and go.
questions.fun_fact: Leonisa started in Medellín and today sells its clothes in many countries across the Americas and Europe.

questions.question: Its Holy Week processions date back to the 16th century and are on UNESCO's heritage list. Which Colombian city holds them?
hints: It's the capital of Cauca, in the country's southwest.
It's known as “the White City.”
Its name starts with P.
questions.description: One week when the whole city walks very slowly, candle in hand.
questions.fun_fact: Popayán's processions were added to UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2009.

questions.question: As Colombian history tells it, at San Mateo in 1814 Antonio Ricaurte destroyed Bolívar's “parque” rather than surrender it. What was it?
wrong_answers: The chest with the troops' pay
hints: In the military language of the time, “parque” didn't mean what it means today.
Ricaurte guarded it in the upper house of the hacienda while Bolívar fought below.
Today you might also call it a magazine, and not the kind you read.
questions.description: A park where nobody ever went on the swings.
questions.fun_fact: Ricaurte was born in Villa de Leyva, and today a town in Cundinamarca and another in Nariño bear his name.

questions.question: In Colombian Sign Language, I’m used for spelling out names that have no sign: each letter is a hand shape. What am I?
hints: Interpreters use it when a name comes up that has no sign.
All you need is one hand and someone watching you.
My name comes from the Greek “dáktylos”, meaning “finger”.
questions.description: An alphabet you don’t read out loud: you watch it, and then you applaud.
questions.fun_fact: Almost every sign language has its own hand alphabet, and they differ from country to country.

review.feedback: The answer "the dactylological alphabet" copies the Spanish "alfabeto dactilológico" word for word. English speakers call it the "manual alphabet" or the "fingerspelling alphabet", so the correct option reads as translationese, and the question becomes a test of Greek roots. A natural version would use "The manual (fingerspelling) alphabet" as the answer. The options and hint 3 would then need new wording, because "manual" comes from the Latin for "hand" and the question already mentions hand shapes.

questions.question: At the Feria de Cali, there is a gathering where caleños and visitors from abroad arrive carrying their most prized treasures. What do they meet for?
questions.answer: To listen to old salsa records
wrong_answers: To choose the queen of the fair
To parade through the city on horseback
hints: Some of them have spent decades hunting for one rare piece.
Many of the people there are older caleños from the city's most salsa-loving neighborhoods.
There are more record players there than dance floors.
questions.description: A Feria de Cali get-together where nobody looks at their phone, and it's not because there's no signal.
questions.fun_fact: Some collectors in Cali own salsa records you can't even find anymore in New York or Puerto Rico.

questions.question: What is the main feature of the steps taught at Cali's salsa schools?
wrong_answers: Slow, long steps like in tango
Soft hip turns like in bolero
Very high jumps like in ballet
hints: The Cali style is famous at world championships.
Dancers at these schools train for years, and many start as children.
Look down: the most impressive part happens close to the floor.
questions.description: In Cali on a Saturday night, there's no empty dance floor and no neighbor asleep.
questions.fun_fact: People say that in Cali, 33 rpm records were played at 45 rpm, and that's why Cali salsa is danced so fast.

questions.question: Jairo Varela founded Grupo Niche and wrote “Cali pachanguero,” but he wasn't from Cali. In which city was he born?
hints: He was born in Colombia's Pacific region.
It's the capital of a very rainy department.
It's the home of chirimía music, on the banks of the Atrato River.
questions.description: He gave Cali so much salsa that the city returned the favor with some giant trumpets.
questions.fun_fact: Cali has a monument to Jairo Varela made of giant metal trumpets, honoring his music.

questions.question: Diana Trujillo, from Cali, led the team behind this Mars rover's robotic arm. What does the robot use that arm for?
questions.answer: To collect and study rocks and soil
wrong_answers: To get back up if it tips over
hints: The robot is like a lab on wheels.
At the tip of the arm there is a drill and several tools.
With it, the rover takes small bits of Martian ground to analyze them.
questions.description: A tourist on another planet who hasn't asked for a vacation in years.
questions.fun_fact: Curiosity has no solar panels: it runs on a nuclear battery that has powered it for more than a decade.

questions.question: The children's ring song “Mambrú se fue a la guerra” makes fun of a real English general. In which century was the song born?
hints: It's from before Colombia's independence.
At that time, France still had kings.
“Mambrú” is how the French said “Marlborough,” a duke who fought in 1709.
questions.description: A children's song about a man who left, and nobody knows when he'll be back.
questions.fun_fact: It became fashionable at the French court when the nanny of Marie Antoinette's son sang it to the baby.

questions.question: In December it's built with moss and little figures, and at midnight on the 24th the Niño Dios is placed in it. Which two animals are with him in the pesebre?
hints: They are farm work animals.
One of them has horns.
The other is the child of a donkey and a mare.
questions.description: The Niño Dios's first neighbors couldn't talk, but they were very cozy and warm.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, these two animals kept the baby warm with their breath on that cold night.

questions.question: One player counts against the wall while the others hide. To save yourself you shout “¡un, dos, tres por mí!” Where must you get to?
questions.answer: The spot where the seeker counted
hints: It's not far away: it's inside the play area.
The seeker has to guard that place while looking for you.
It's the wall or post where the counting happened.
questions.description: The only game where losing means you got found.
questions.fun_fact: If the last player shouted “¡por mí y por todos mis compañeros!” (for me and all my friends), the whole team was set free.

questions.question: One morning I went out all stiff and dapper, in short pants and a ribboned hat, even though my mom told me not to go. Who am I?
hints: I appear in a poem by Rafael Pombo.
I live near the water.
My mom is a frog.
questions.description: A stroll that started out very fancy and ended very badly.
questions.fun_fact: Pombo was inspired by an old English nursery song about a frog who goes courting.

questions.question: Who is this Colombian writer?
hints: He was born in Aracataca, Magdalena.
His face is on the 50,000-peso note.
He wrote “One Hundred Years of Solitude.”
questions.description: A famous mustache that isn't Juan Valdez's.
questions.fun_fact: To receive the Nobel Prize in 1982, Gabo skipped the tailcoat and wore a white liquiliqui, a traditional Caribbean suit.

questions.question: In many Colombian classrooms, first graders use the Nacho workbook. What do they learn with it?
hints: It starts with the vowels.
It has syllables like “ma, me, mi, mo, mu.”
Its full title is “Nacho lee.”
questions.description: Many Colombians' very first book is named like a kid from the neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: It's published by a Medellín publisher, and several generations of Colombians have learned with it.

questions.question: In Colombia, homes are ranked into estratos (social levels) based on the neighborhood. How many estratos are there?
hints: The lowest one is estrato 1.
They are used to work out how much you pay for water, power and gas.
More than five and fewer than ten.
questions.description: The favorite question of anyone about to rent you an apartment.
questions.fun_fact: Homes in estratos 5 and 6 pay more for water, power and gas to help cover the bills of estratos 1, 2 and 3.

questions.question: Every July 20 there are parades, flags everywhere and no school. What does Colombia celebrate?
hints: It's a national holiday.
It recalls the cry for freedom of 1810 in Bogotá.
On that day Colombia began breaking away from Spain.
questions.description: The one day a year when the whole country puts on its yellow, blue and red uniform.
questions.fun_fact: It all started with a fight because a Spanish merchant refused to lend a flower vase in the main square of Bogotá.

questions.question: In Boyacá and the Bogotá savanna, farmers fear the “heladas.” What is a helada?
questions.answer: A pre-dawn cold that freezes the crops
wrong_answers: A downpour of small falling balls of ice
A snowfall that turns the towns white
A very strong wind that knocks plants over
hints: It happens mostly on clear nights with no clouds.
It usually comes in the dry season, from December to February.
At dawn the grass looks white and the plants' leaves look burned.
questions.description: An enemy of Boyacá's potatoes, feared even more than the worms.
questions.fun_fact: Cloudless nights are the most dangerous: without that “blanket,” the ground's heat escapes to the sky and the temperature can drop below freezing.

questions.question: Colombia's Evelis Aguilar competes in the heptathlon. Which of these events is one of its seven?
hints: The heptathlon has three races, two jumps and two throws.
The two throws are the shot put and one more.
The object thrown is long and has a pointed tip.
questions.description: Seven events in two days: the perfect plan for anyone who gets bored fast.
questions.fun_fact: The heptathlon events are the 100 m hurdles, high jump, shot put, 200 m, long jump, javelin and 800 m.

questions.question: Bogotá has two letters after its name, isn't part of Cundinamarca and is split into 20 localities. What is Bogotá on the political map?
hints: It has its own mayor and its own city council.
The two letters are the same ones Washington has in the United States.
The letters are D.C.
questions.description: It's the capital of a department, but it doesn't pay that department any rent.
questions.fun_fact: Even though it isn't part of Cundinamarca, Bogotá is still that department's capital.

questions.question: General Gustavo Rojas Pinilla fell from power on May 10, 1957. Who took power in his place?
hints: Elections didn't come right away.
They governed until August 1958, when Alberto Lleras Camargo took office.
They were four generals and a rear admiral, led by Gabriel París.
questions.description: One May when Colombia changed governments without waiting for an election.
questions.fun_fact: Those days are remembered as the “Jornadas de Mayo” (May Days), with strikes by students, banks and shops.

questions.question: You're in a colonial house in Popayán and someone says, “Vamos al patio.” What is the patio?
questions.answer: The open space in the middle of the house
hints: From there you can see the sky.
It often has plants, flowers and sometimes a stone water basin.
All the rooms open onto it, all the way around.
questions.description: An everyday word that, in Popayán, carries centuries of history.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish brought the central patio with them, and they had learned it from Arab and Roman houses.

questions.question: The Inquisition in Cartagena put women from Tolú on trial for going to “aquelarres”, witches' night meetings. What language does that word come from?
hints: It's a language older than Spanish.
It's so old that nobody really knows where it came from.
It's spoken in Bilbao and San Sebastián.
questions.description: A neighborhood meeting where nobody takes the bus: everyone flies in on a broom.
questions.fun_fact: The best-known explanation is that “aquelarre” comes from “akelarre”, which would mean ‘meadow of the billy goat’ in Basque.

questions.question: On the Caribbean coast, a beach vendor fondly calls a lady “mi reina”. What does he call a man?
hints: It’s the highest title in a palace.
The queen marries him.
It’s the partner of “mi reina”.
questions.description: On the beach nobody wears a crown, but everyone has a title.
questions.fun_fact: In Cali and on the coast, people say “mi rey” and “mi reina” even to someone they’ve just met.

questions.question: In many bakeries, pandebono comes filled with a firm, reddish, sweet paste that's cut into slices. Which one?
hints: It's also used to fill roscones and obleas.
It's sold in blocks or small bars that you cut with a knife.
With cheese, it becomes a classic of the onces (afternoon snack).
questions.description: A cheese bread that decided it wanted to be dessert too.
questions.fun_fact: Pandebono is made with cassava starch, cheese and egg, with no wheat flour at all.

questions.question: At a Colombian bakery, you order an alfajor. What do you get?
questions.answer: Two soft cookies joined with arequipe
wrong_answers: A round bread roll filled with bocadillo
A sponge cake roll filled with jam
A puff pastry cake with cream
hints: You eat it in one or two bites.
Sometimes the outside is covered in grated coconut or powdered sugar.
It has two little lids with a brown filling in the middle.
questions.description: The treat nobody eats just one of, even when they swear they will.
questions.fun_fact: The word alfajor comes from Arabic, and the treat reached the Americas from Spain.

questions.question: Which marimba player born in Guapi founded Grupo Bahía, which took the Pacific's currulao to stages around the world?
hints: He's from Cauca and is also a composer and producer.
He's not a mid-20th-century pioneer: his career took off in the 1990s.
His second given name sounds like “candela,” Spanish for fire.
questions.description: A man who gets more music out of wood than a carpenter with the hiccups.
questions.fun_fact: The keys of the marimba de chonta are made from chonta palm wood, and its resonators from guadua bamboo tubes.

questions.question: Emilio Fortou founded it in 1945. It recorded Pacho Galán and was a rival of Discos Fuentes. In which city was the Discos Tropical label born?
hints: It is a city on the Caribbean coast.
In the 1940s and 1950s, it was a big center for orchestras and radio stations.
It is the city of Colombia's most famous Carnival.
questions.description: Before Spotify, music from the coast lived on black plates that went round and round.
questions.fun_fact: Discos Fuentes started in Cartagena and later moved to Medellín, but Discos Tropical always stayed a Barranquilla label.

questions.question: When a player lifts the ball over an opponent's head and collects it on the other side, Colombians say they pulled off a…
hints: The move humiliates the defender a little.
The ball goes over, not under.
It's something you wear on your head, in diminutive form.
questions.description: A move so elegant that the opponent ends up staring at the clouds.
questions.fun_fact: The chalaca, another famous move, is named after the port of Callao in Peru, where it is said to have been born.

questions.question: Obleas are two thin, round wafers. What classic sweet gets spread in the middle?
hints: It's sweet, not salty.
It's light brown and sticky.
It's made by cooking milk with sugar for a long time.
questions.description: Two wafers so thin they need glue to keep from flying away.
questions.fun_fact: Obleas can also get grated cheese, blackberry jam and even cream, all at once.

questions.question: Which of these does NOT appear on the flag of Cartagena?
hints: The flag has three colors in rectangles, one inside the other.
Barranquilla has an almost identical flag.
Its colors are red, yellow and green.
questions.description: A flag that stacks boxes inside boxes, like a Russian nesting doll.
questions.fun_fact: This flag is nicknamed “la cuadrilonga,” and it flew during Cartagena's independence in 1811.

questions.question: It's 1863 in Rionegro: the Liberals who won the 1860–1862 civil war write a new constitution. What do they name the country?
hints: The country was split into nine sovereign states.
Its great promoter was General Tomás Cipriano de Mosquera.
It copies the official name of the country whose capital is Washington.
questions.description: A country that changed its name more often than its president.
questions.fun_fact: The country kept that name for 23 years, until the Constitution of 1886 changed it to Republic of Colombia.

questions.question: This is what bills look like before they're cut. What are the bills printed by the Banco de la República mainly made of?
hints: It isn't the same paper as in your notebooks.
That's why they hold up better if you forget them in a pocket and they go through the wash.
It's the same fiber your T-shirts are made of.
questions.description: Literally making money, and it's not even a crime.
questions.fun_fact: The Banco de la República has its own banknote printing plant in Bogotá.

questions.question: Look at the photo: these flower pots are made of reddish fired clay with no glaze. What is this material called?
hints: It's a type of ceramic.
Its name comes from Italian and means something like “baked earth.”
China's famous clay army of warriors, guarding an emperor's tomb, is made of it.
questions.description: Grandma's plants live better than most of us, each in its own little clay house.
questions.fun_fact: Clay pots let the soil breathe, because water and air pass through their tiny pores.

questions.question: In Usiacurí, Atlántico, people weave famous colorful crafts. From which fiber?
hints: The fiber is cut into thin strips and dyed in bright colors.
Hats are woven from this same fiber in Sandoná, Nariño.
Ecuador's famous “Panama” hat is woven from this same palm.
questions.description: In this town in Atlántico, hands work faster than the ceiling fan.
questions.fun_fact: The poet Julio Flórez spent his last years in Usiacurí, and his house is now a museum.

questions.question: The Serranía de Chiribiquete has tens of thousands of red rock paintings showing jaguars and deer. What was the red color made from?
questions.answer: An iron-rich mineral from the earth
hints: The ancient painters used whatever they found around the tepuis.
That's why it has lasted thousands of years without fading.
It's called ochre.
questions.description: Colombia's first decorated wall, and nobody got fined for drawing on it.
questions.fun_fact: Chiribiquete was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2018, for both its nature and its culture.

questions.question: In Colombia it's called patilla: big, green and striped outside, red with black seeds inside. What is it almost entirely made of?
hints: There's a reason people eat so much of it in the hot lowlands.
When you bite into it, it drips down your chin.
It's the same thing that comes out of the faucet.
questions.description: A fruit so big you have to carry it like a baby.
questions.fun_fact: Patilla is about 92% water, which is why it quenches your thirst almost as well as a glass of water.

questions.question: I'm not a prayer or a charm, and I cost nothing. If a spirit gets you lost in the hills, I break the spell and you find your way. What am I?
wrong_answers: Wearing your shoes on the wrong feet
hints: It works against the duende and the Madremonte.
You do it to yourself, with what you have on.
The seams end up on the outside.
questions.description: The countryside's free GPS for when spirits hide the path from you.
questions.fun_fact: Country folk say the duende is especially fond of girls with long hair and of children.

review.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. Turning clothes inside out is the well-known remedy against the duende and Madremonte when lost. The duende is said to like children and long-haired girls, which is plausible. I did not run a search, so I couldn't confirm that every wrong answer is absent from the folklore (e.g. shoes on the wrong feet).

questions.question: You go out with binoculars. In which of these places in Colombia would you NOT see a condor flying free?
wrong_answers: The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta
hints: The condor needs high mountains and strong winds.
Its full name, “Andean condor,” tells you where it lives.
One of these places is low, hot jungle.
questions.description: A bird so big that if it landed on your balcony, you'd have to ask it to scoot over.
questions.fun_fact: The Andean condor's wings can measure more than 3 meters (10 ft) from tip to tip.

questions.question: Look at the photo: when the anthem plays at school, many people put their hand like this. What are they showing with it?
hints: People also do it when the flag is raised.
It's a way to honor your country.
It's the same thing you show when you listen carefully to your teacher.
questions.description: A gesture that doesn't say a single word, and still everyone understands it.
questions.fun_fact: The right hand goes over the left side of the chest, where the heart is.

questions.question: From 1968 I managed Colombia's natural resources and created many national parks; in 1993 the Ministry of the Environment replaced me. What was my name?
hints: I was a government institute.
My name was an acronym that started with “In”.
My acronym included “recursos naturales renovables” (renewable natural resources).
questions.description: An acronym that sounds like a tongue twister and looked after half the country.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's first national park, Cueva de los Guácharos, was created in 1960, before this institute even existed.

questions.question: Look at the photo: the carbonero flower looks like a red pom-pom. What are those red “hairs” really?
hints: They have to do with how the plant reproduces.
At the tip of each “hair” there's a tiny bit of pollen.
They are the male part of the flower.
questions.description: A flower that got its hair done for the party, and now every strand is standing on end.
questions.fun_fact: The carbonero's petals are so tiny and greenish that hardly anyone notices them.

questions.question: I’m a woman from Colombia’s Pacific coast: in the arrullos I sing the lead and the others answer me in chorus, to the cununo drum. What am I?
hints: You find me at wakes and saints’ festivals in Guapi, Timbiquí or Tumaco.
The women who answer me in the chorus are called “respondedoras.”
My name comes from the Spanish verb for what I do with my throat.
questions.description: In Guapi, the marimba, the cununo and the downpour never take a day off.
questions.fun_fact: In 2010, UNESCO declared the marimba music and traditional chants of Colombia’s South Pacific region an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: It comes from Quechua, you hear it in Pasto and in Ecuador, and it means a baby still carried in arms. What's the word?
hints: Grandmothers in southern Colombia use this word all the time.
In Cuba, this same word means a bus.
It sounds almost like a baby crying.
questions.description: Sleeps all day, eats every three hours and runs the whole house.
questions.fun_fact: In Cuba and the Canary Islands a “guagua” is a bus, so if you ask for one in Havana, nobody will hand you a baby.

questions.question: You shake me before using me, I let out colored paint, and graffiti artists use me on the walls of Bogotá. What am I?
hints: I'm made of metal.
Inside me there's a little ball that rattles when you shake me.
Press the little button on top and the paint comes out as a fine mist.
questions.description: A street artist without this is like a goalkeeper without gloves.
questions.fun_fact: Spray paint cans have a little ball inside that mixes the paint when you shake them: that's why they go “clack, clack”.

questions.question: The yipao is a Willys jeep loaded to the roof with coffee, plantains or a family’s furniture, and it has its own parade. In which department did that parade begin?
hints: It’s one of Colombia’s smallest departments.
The Cocora Valley, with its wax palms, is there.
Its capital is Armenia.
questions.description: A car that carries more than a mule and never asks for a break.
questions.fun_fact: In the Coffee Axis, “un yipao” is also a unit of measure: whatever fits in a fully loaded Willys.

questions.question: In many versions of the tale, a doll is placed on Tío Conejo’s path to catch him. What is it made of?
hints: The rabbit hits the doll because it doesn’t answer his greeting.
With every blow he gets more stuck: his paws won’t come loose.
It’s the sticky black stuff once used to seal wooden ships.
questions.description: Tío Conejo learned the hard way that not everyone who stays quiet is a friend.
questions.fun_fact: The same tale exists in the southern United States, where the doll is called the “Tar-Baby” and the one who falls for the trap is Br’er Rabbit.

questions.question: Camilo released “Vida de rico” (“A Rich Man's Life”) in 2020. What does the song's title mean?
questions.answer: That love makes him feel rich
wrong_answers: That he misses simple life in his hometown
hints: Camilo is known for his cheerful, simple style.
It became one of his catchiest songs of those years.
What makes him rich is being with the person he loves.
questions.description: A song you sing with a ukulele and an ear-to-ear grin.
questions.fun_fact: Camilo sings many of his love songs with Evaluna, his wife, in mind, and she also appears in his videos.

questions.question: This charro in the photo is a must at every Colombian party. Who is he?
hints: He was born in Jalisco and sang for more than 50 years.
He is known as “the King of ranchera music.”
His version of “El rey” by José Alfredo Jiménez is the most famous one.
questions.description: At Colombian parties, around midnight, this Mexican guest always shows up.
questions.fun_fact: His most famous line was that as long as the audience kept clapping, he would keep singing.

questions.question: In 1804 a Spanish expedition reached Cartagena with a vaccine passed from arm to arm among children. Which disease was it against?
hints: It left marks on the skin of those who survived.
No mosquito spreads it.
It was the first human disease wiped off the planet, in 1980.
questions.description: A trip across the Atlantic where the smallest passengers were the most important ones.
questions.fun_fact: The word “vaccine” comes from the Latin “vacca”, meaning cow, because the first one was made from cowpox.

questions.question: Fernando Gómez Agudelo organized Colombia's first television broadcast. In what year was it?
hints: It was in the 1950s.
General Gustavo Rojas Pinilla was in power.
It was on June 13, exactly one year after Rojas Pinilla took power in 1953.
questions.description: Before this, Colombians could only hear their telenovelas, not watch them.
questions.fun_fact: Almost nobody in Colombia owned a TV for that first broadcast, so the government put sets in shop windows for people to watch from the street.

questions.question: It's the most typical shout of vallenato singers, heard right before a verse: “¡Ay, …!” What completes it?
hints: You hear it in almost every vallenato song, old or new.
On the coast people shorten their words, and this one lost a letter along the way.
It's “hombre,” said the coastal way, without the r.
questions.description: The official sigh of every heartbroken singer with an accordion by his side.
questions.fun_fact: “Hombe” is the coastal way of saying “hombre” (man), and in vallenato it can express joy, longing or heartbreak, depending on how it's sung.

questions.question: Which singer and actor played Diomedes Díaz in the 2015 TV series “Diomedes, el Cacique de La Junta”?
hints: The series aired on Canal RCN.
The lead actor is also a vallenato singer, born in the Caribbean region.
His last name starts with L.
questions.description: Stepping into the Cacique's shoes isn't easy: you have to sing, act and put up with the comparisons.
questions.fun_fact: The nickname “el Cacique de La Junta” comes from La Junta, the village in La Guajira where Diomedes Díaz was from.

questions.question: The Desfile Magno, with its giant floats, closes the Carnaval de Negros y Blancos on Día de Blancos. What day in January is it?
hints: First comes Día de Negros, then Día de Blancos.
It falls in the first week of January.
It’s the same day as Three Kings’ Day.
questions.description: The biggest floats in southern Colombia, and not one of them fits in the garage.
questions.fun_fact: In 2009, UNESCO added the Carnaval de Negros y Blancos to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: It goes on the living room floor or next to the bed, it's woven from wool or other fibers, and it's what Colombians call a small rug. What's the word?
hints: It keeps your feet off the cold floor when you get up.
People shake it outside to get the dust out.
It starts with “ta.”
questions.description: That thing in the house everyone swears they shook out last week.
questions.fun_fact: The oldest known knotted rug, the Pazyryk carpet, is about 2,400 years old and was found frozen in the Altai Mountains of Siberia.

questions.question: The word “jaibaná” names the wise person who heals with chants and talks with spirits. Which Indigenous people does it come from?
hints: They are a people of the rainforests of Colombia's Pacific coast.
Many of their communities live in Chocó, near the Atrato River.
Their women are famous for bead necklaces and body paint made from jagua fruit.
questions.description: A doctor who prescribes no pills, only chants and spirits.
questions.fun_fact: Emberá jaibanás use wooden staffs carved with figures to talk with the spirits.

questions.question: Which of these countries does NOT share a border with Colombia?
hints: Think of the map: three of these countries touch Colombia somewhere.
In this country, many people speak Guaraní as well as Spanish.
Its capital is Asunción.
questions.description: Some neighbors lend you sugar; others you only run into in World Cup qualifiers.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia shares borders with five countries: Venezuela, Brazil, Peru, Ecuador and Panama.

questions.question: Colombia's national team is called “la Tricolor”. Why?
questions.answer: For the three colors of the flag
wrong_answers: For the three stars on its jersey
For its three Copa América titles
hints: “Tri” means three.
The nickname has nothing to do with trophies or titles.
Yellow, blue and red.
questions.description: National teams have more nicknames than Grandma has grandchildren.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia has won only one Copa América, in 2001, played at home.

questions.question: In San Gil, before rafting on the Fonce River, you get a life jacket. What is it for?
questions.answer: To float if you fall in the water
wrong_answers: To keep you from getting cold
hints: It's for your safety.
It's filled with a very light material.
If the boat flips over, it won't let you sink.
questions.description: In that loud orange, even the fish in the Fonce will recognize you.
questions.fun_fact: San Gil, in Santander, is called Colombia's capital of adventure tourism.

questions.question: “Parce” is to Medellín as … is to Cali.
hints: “Parce” is what you call a friend.
You're looking for what someone from Cali calls a friend.
It sounds a lot like “compa”.
questions.description: Every city has its own name for the person who sticks with you through everything.
questions.fun_fact: In Barranquilla, on the other hand, a friend is called “cuadro”.

questions.question: Bogotá-born artist María Fernanda Cardoso, who lives in Australia, ran a real circus with tiny performers she trained herself. What animals were they?
hints: They were insects.
They have no wings, but they jump a huge distance.
They often live in the fur of dogs and cats.
questions.description: A show where the performers are so tiny it's hard to know where to clap.
questions.fun_fact: The fleas in Cardoso's circus pulled little carts and walked the tightrope, and the show was seen in museums in several countries.

questions.question: Profesor Yarumo teaches about farm life on Colombian TV. What is the yarumo his name comes from?
hints: It is very common in the Colombian mountains.
Sloths love to eat it.
It has big leaves, like open hands, silvery underneath.
questions.description: A teacher who knows more about the countryside than a retired cow.
questions.fun_fact: The white yarumo has silvery leaves you can spot from far away on the mountainsides, and it is one of sloths' favorite foods.

questions.question: Around Malpelo Island, divers see schools of hammerhead sharks. How many come together in the biggest schools?
hints: It's one of the best places in the world to see them.
Divers say they block out the sunlight.
They number far more than a hundred.
questions.description: A fish that went to the hardware store and walked out wearing the tool.
questions.fun_fact: Malpelo is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, partly because of its huge schools of sharks.

questions.question: In 1813, the Free State of Cartagena made me a town and gave me a coat of arms as a reward for backing independence. Which city am I?
hints: I sit on the banks of the Magdalena River.
The motto on my coat of arms is “Premio al patriotismo” (Reward for Patriotism).
Today I'm the capital of Atlántico.
questions.description: A coat of arms handed out like a gold star for good patriotic behavior.
questions.fun_fact: The coat of arms was granted by Manuel Rodríguez Torices, president of the Free State of Cartagena, while Santa Marta was still on the king's side.

questions.question: In the biographical telenovela “Pambelé,” Antonio Cervantes becomes Colombia's first world boxing champion. In what year did that really happen?
hints: It was more than 50 years ago.
It happened in the 1970s, in a fight in Panama.
It was two years after the 1970 World Cup in Mexico.
questions.description: A knockout of a story that had the whole country yelling at the TV.
questions.fun_fact: Kid Pambelé was born in San Basilio de Palenque, considered the first free town in the Americas.

questions.question: If you want to see the Festival Folclórico y Reinado Nacional del Bambuco in Neiva, which month do you travel?
hints: It's in the middle of the year.
The streets fill with parades, bambuco music and asado huilense.
It's the month when the mid-year school vacation starts at many Colombian schools.
questions.description: A party where queens are crowned not just for their looks, but also for how they move their feet.
questions.fun_fact: In the pageant, every candidate has to dance the sanjuanero huilense in front of the judges.

questions.question: In Colombia, what do you call the number 10 position that plays behind the strikers and sets up goals, like el Pibe Valderrama?
hints: My spot is in the middle of the field.
I’m not the one who wins the ball back: I hand it out.
In other countries they call me “enganche” or “armador”; in English, a playmaker.
questions.description: Some jerseys weigh more than others, even when they’re made of the same fabric.
questions.fun_fact: The 10 became the number of soccer magicians thanks to Pelé, who wore it almost by chance at the 1958 World Cup.

questions.question: I'm a region of flat savannas, my rivers flow to the Orinoco, and my men wear a liqui liqui and a hat to parties. Which region am I?
hints: I share these savannas with Venezuela.
Joropo is danced here with harp, cuatro and maracas.
Villavicencio is my gateway.
questions.description: An outfit so elegant it works for herding cattle and for accepting a Nobel Prize.
questions.fun_fact: The liqui liqui is typical of the plains of Colombia and Venezuela, and in Venezuela it's considered the national men's outfit.

questions.question: I'm a goalkeeper. I played for Arsenal in England and Napoli in Italy, and I started in goal for Colombia at the 2014 and 2018 World Cups. Who am I?
hints: I was born in Medellín in 1988.
I have played more matches for Colombia than anyone else in history.
I share my first name with the boy who beat the giant Goliath.
questions.description: A man whose whole job is making sure nothing happens.
questions.fun_fact: Ospina played more than 120 matches for Colombia, more than any other player.

review.feedback: Source: hint 2 and the fun fact say Ospina has played more matches for Colombia than anyone else. That record can change, and by late 2026 James Rodríguez may have passed his roughly 128 caps, so I can't confirm it is still true. Rephrase it in the source (for example "one of the most-capped players in Colombia's history" or "more than 120 matches"), then translate it again. Apart from that, the translation is faithful and reads naturally.

questions.question: I spin round and round on the Kokoriko rotisserie until I’m golden, and I’m served with potatoes and arepa. What am I?
hints: I’m an animal with feathers.
Before the rotisserie, I lived on a farm and scratched at the dirt.
The name “Kokoriko” sounds like a rooster’s crow.
questions.description: For many Colombians, Sunday lunch smells of charcoal and family.
questions.fun_fact: The name Kokoriko imitates a rooster’s crow as it sounds in some languages, a cousin of English “cock-a-doodle-doo.”

questions.question: The Spanish built it on San Lázaro Hill in Cartagena, with sloping walls and tunnels inside. What for?
questions.answer: To defend the city from pirates and enemy armies
wrong_answers: To house the viceroy and his family
To store gold before shipping it to Spain
hints: From the top you could see everything arriving by land and by sea.
Its name recalls a king of Spain, Philip IV.
It has cannons pointing outward.
questions.description: A castle with no princesses or dragons, but a very unfriendly face.
questions.fun_fact: It is said to be the largest fortress the Spanish built in their American colonies.

questions.question: In Colombia, what do people call the loud, blunt, direct way of talking of people from Santander?
hints: If you're not used to it, it feels like you're being told off.
It's the exact opposite of a soft, sing-song way of talking.
It sounds as if every word lands a punch.
questions.description: Some accents sound like a scolding even when they're offering you lunch.
questions.fun_fact: Many people from Santander explain that they're not angry at all: that's just how they talk.

questions.question: Look at the map: the highlighted department is home to El Totumo volcano, where people float in mud. Which one is it?
hints: It's on the Caribbean coast.
Mompox, the town by the Magdalena River, is in this department too.
Its capital is Cartagena, the walled city.
questions.description: A natural spa where the mud mask covers you from head to toe.
questions.fun_fact: It's almost impossible to sink in El Totumo's mud: it's so thick that you float like a cork.

questions.question: “I live in the Tatacoa Desert, in Huila. At night, people come to look at the stars with me.” What am I?
hints: My work starts when the sun goes down.
From me you can see planets, the Moon and shooting stars.
Inside, I have telescopes.
questions.description: There's not much to see in the desert by day, but at night the show is free and has millions of lights.
questions.fun_fact: La Tatacoa is one of the best places in Colombia for stargazing because there are few clouds and almost no city lights reach it.

questions.question: Colombian Éider Arévalo became world champion in 2017 in the track and field event shown in the photo. Which one is it?
hints: The judges watch very closely how the athletes move their legs.
Its classic Olympic distances were 20 km and 50 km.
Both feet must never leave the ground at the same time.
questions.description: A sport for people in a big hurry with even bigger patience.
questions.fun_fact: In race walking, the supporting leg must stay straight from the moment it touches the ground until it passes under the body.

questions.question: Bogotá's main square faces the Capitol and the Cathedral. Who is it named after?
hints: He is a hero of Independence.
He is called “the Liberator.”
A department on the Caribbean coast carries his surname.
questions.description: The living room of every Colombian's home, pigeons included.
questions.fun_fact: The Bolívar statue in the middle of the square dates from 1846 and is Bogotá's oldest public monument.

questions.question: I have colorful wings, and at the Quindío Botanical Garden I live with hundreds of others in a huge house. What am I?
hints: I love drinking nectar from flowers.
Before I could fly, I spent some time sitting still inside a chrysalis.
Before I had wings, I was a caterpillar.
questions.description: A glass house where the tenants pay no rent and fly in through the door.
questions.fun_fact: Seen from above, the butterfly house at the Quindío Botanical Garden in Calarcá is shaped like a butterfly.

questions.question: I have four thick strings, I'm almost as tall as a person, I'm played standing up, and I have the lowest sound in the string orchestra. What am I?
hints: You'll also find me in lots of jazz bands.
I can be played with a bow or by plucking the strings.
My name starts with a word that means “twice.”
questions.description: In the orchestra everyone follows the conductor, though some pretend they can't see him.
questions.fun_fact: In many Colombian estudiantinas, the double bass joins tiples, bandolas and guitars to add the low notes.

questions.question: In the San Andrés and Providencia archipelago there is a place called Quitasueño. What is it?
hints: It lies far from the inhabited islands, north of Providencia.
Almost all of it is underwater.
Ships fear it because they can run aground there.
questions.description: A name that sounds like the herbal tea grandma makes you before bed.
questions.fun_fact: In 2012, the International Court of Justice confirmed that Quitasueño belongs to Colombia, in its dispute with Nicaragua.

questions.question: The Perseverance rover, which Colombian Diana Trujillo worked on, landed in Jezero Crater. Why did NASA choose it? Because long ago there was…
hints: NASA was looking for a place where tiny life might have existed long ago.
From orbit you can see a delta, like the one a river makes where it ends.
Still water sat there billions of years ago.
questions.description: To pick a landing spot on Mars, NASA had to look very, very far back in time.
questions.fun_fact: Perseverance stores rock samples in sealed tubes so a future mission can bring them back to Earth.

questions.question: In Bogotá and Medellín, depending on the day of the week, some cars can't be driven at the busiest hours. What is this rule called?
hints: It changes with the day of the week.
It depends on the numbers on the front and back of the car.
Its name joins the Spanish for “rush hour” with the Spanish for what shows a car's number.
questions.description: The rule that makes your dad check the calendar before taking the car out.
questions.fun_fact: Bogotá started pico y placa in 1998, and many other Colombian cities later copied the idea.

questions.question: It's measured in points every night, and if it's too low, a telenovela can be taken off the air. What is it?
hints: It shows up in the entertainment news the next day.
Caracol and RCN fight over it every night.
It's how many people are tuned in to a TV show.
questions.description: Telenovela producers bite their nails the morning after every premiere because of this.
questions.fun_fact: “Yo soy Betty, la fea” reached some of the highest ratings in the history of Colombian television.
